## Policy Synthesis Regimes {#sec-training-synthesis-regimes}

The latch task could draw on four sources of experience: the teleoperated door openings of @sec-data, a log of imperfect or scripted door runs, a simulator of the cage door, and the arm itself. Each buys a different capability at a different physical price, and @tbl-06-regimes sets them side by side with the failure each is known for and the check that intercepts it.

| Policy Synthesis Regime            | Core Purchased Capability                                                                                        | Data & Compute Budget                                                 | Sample Efficiency & Scale                            | Hardware Safety & Wear Risk                                                           | Dominant Failure Mode & Interceptor                                                                                                                 |
|:-----------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Behavioral Cloning (BC)**        | Imitates attributable expert actions                                                                             | Expert collection, curation, and supervised optimization              | Limited by coverage and operator availability        | Optimization adds no physical exploration; collection still incurs exposure           | Mode averaging and missing recovery. Multimodal decoding and new expert labels address training; qualified state and action limits bound execution. |
| **Offline / Batch RL**             | Uses rewards to select behavior from heterogeneous logs                                                          | Logged transitions with rewards and state-action coverage             | Reuses recorded experience without new online trials | Optimization adds no exploration; the archive inherits collection risks               | Unsupported action values. Conservative objectives reduce optimism; independent action limits remain necessary.                                     |
| **Sim-to-Real RL**                 | Explores behavior through simulated interaction; a privileged teacher can be distilled into a deployable student | Parallel rollout compute plus physical calibration and transfer tests | Throughput depends on task, solver, and hardware     | Simulation avoids training wear; physical probing and deployment still incur exposure | Solver exploitation and omitted mechanisms. Paired probes qualify the simulator; approach and force limits need their own response evidence.        |
| **Residual RL & Real Fine-Tuning** | Adapts to local physical mismatch                                                                                | Machine interaction, resets, cooling, and regression testing          | Physical trials make sample efficiency consequential | Contact loads and thermal exposure accumulate during adaptation                       | Local improvement with regression elsewhere. Independent residual gates limit authority; combined-controller tests assess the change.               |

: **Comparative trade-off matrix across policy synthesis regimes**: The four regimes compared are behavioral cloning, offline reinforcement learning, sim-to-real reinforcement learning, and residual RL/fine-tuning. Columns separate the capability sought, the resources that determine its cost, and the remaining failure mechanism. Training remedies and physical execution safeguards have different roles; neither supplies the other's evidence. {#tbl-06-regimes tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

For the latch campaign, **behavioral cloning**\index{Behavioral cloning} directly uses the expert actions already available and avoids designing a reward for the nominal opening. It frames policy synthesis as supervised regression or classification over a collected dataset of expert state-action pairs $\mathcal{D} = \{(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)\}$. Following the action taps of @sec-data-action-label, a demonstration dataset pairs observations with either the operator's mapped setpoints or the setpoints the permission path admitted:
$$\mathcal{D}_{\text{intent}} = \left\{ \left(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{a}_{\text{cmd}, t:t+H-1}\right) \right\} \quad \text{vs.} \quad \mathcal{D}_{\text{verified}} = \left\{ \left(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{a}_{\text{enf}, t:t+H-1}\right) \right\}$$
Cloning the mapped setpoints ($\mathbf{a}_{\text{cmd}}$) teaches the operator's requests in the robot's coordinates before permission checks. Cloning the admitted setpoints ($\mathbf{a}_{\text{enf}}$) also teaches the modifications made by that particular permission path. Neither tap automatically supplies an expert target: curation must establish who controlled the action, whether the sequence demonstrates the intended behavior, and which interventions altered it. A learner's rejected command remains failure evidence; an attributable expert recovery can become a separate training sequence. Learning admitted actions can reduce repeated disagreement with the permission path, but couples the policy to its limits and deceleration profiles. Learning mapped requests preserves the distinction between intent and enforcement, but can require more intervention at runtime. In its standard formulation, the optimization objective minimizes a multi-step prediction loss over continuous action sequences drawn from demonstration trajectories (see @sec-appendix-ml-multimodal for classical regression formulations).[^fn-hist-alvinn-cloning]
Because this loss penalizes only the discrepancy between the commanded action and the recorded demonstration at observed states, the training objective does not evaluate task completion, terminal cost, or the stability of the closed-loop dynamical system. It fits actions to observations only.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ The four-stream action tap tuple separating intent from enforcement is formulated in @sec-data-action-label.
:::

[^fn-hist-alvinn-cloning]: **ALVINN road perspective warping**\index{ALVINN}: Pomerleau's Autonomous Land Vehicle in a Neural Network (ALVINN) [@pomerleau1989alvinn], told in @sec-data-collection-sources, drifted toward the lane edge because its human drivers never demonstrated a recovery from it. To supply recovery examples without unsafe driving, Pomerleau used synthetic perspective warping, rendering laterally shifted and rotated road images paired with transformed steering corrections, an early case of augmenting demonstrations with recovery data off the nominal trajectory.

### The multimodality breakdown and mode averaging {#sec-training-multimodality-breakdown}

When human demonstrators execute a physical task, their strategy is frequently multimodal. Consider an obstacle avoidance scenario where an embodied mobile manipulator navigates toward a goal blocked by a central structural column. A human teleoperator may choose to steer around the column to the left in half of the demonstrations, or to the right in the remaining half. The recorded demonstration archive $\mathcal{D}$ contains two distinct, dynamically valid trajectories, but precisely zero examples of driving straight down the center line into the obstacle.

A deterministic point-regression behavioral cloning policy cannot represent both modes for the same observation $\mathbf{o}$. Under empirical mean squared error ($L_2$) loss, the network optimizes:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{a}) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \left\| \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{o}) - \mathbf{a} \right\|_2^2 \right].$$
The theoretical minimizer of this objective is the conditional expectation of the action distribution (for the formal derivation, see @sec-appendix-ml-multimodal):[^fn-math-mode-averaging]
$$\pi^*(\mathbf{o}) = \arg\min_{\hat{\mathbf{a}}} \int \|\hat{\mathbf{a}} - \mathbf{a}\|_2^2\,p(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o})\,d\mathbf{a} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o}] = \int \mathbf{a}\,p(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o})\,d\mathbf{a}.$$
In conventional computer vision, predicting the conditional mean of ambiguous pixel targets generates blurry, averaged textures; in natural language processing, it produces diffused semantic embeddings. In Physical AI, however, the conditional expectation of two collision-free evasion commands (such as $\mathbf{a}_{\text{left}} = [v_x, +\omega_z]^\top$ and $\mathbf{a}_{\text{right}} = [v_x, -\omega_z]^\top$, where $v_x$ is forward linear speed and $\omega_z$ is angular yaw rate) evaluates to:
$$\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o}] = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_{\text{left}} + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}_{\text{right}} = \left[ v_x, 0.0 \right]^\top.$$
The regression mean proposes forward motion with zero lateral evasion. If admitted unchanged, that proposal heads toward the central obstacle.

This invalid proposal is not caused by an optimization pathology, insufficient model capacity, vanishing gradients, or dataset scarcity. It is the mathematically exact, optimal solution to a point-regression loss evaluated over a multimodal physical distribution. The Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives of the loss with respect to the proposed action; a positive-definite Hessian establishes a unique minimum in that action space. This is a statement about the optimal output, not about whether neural-network weight optimization is convex. The loss landscape $\mathcal{R}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}) = \int \|\hat{\mathbf{a}} - \mathbf{a}\|_2^2 p(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o})\,d\mathbf{a}$ is strictly convex with respect to the output action vector $\hat{\mathbf{a}}$, with Hessian $\nabla^2_{\hat{\mathbf{a}}} \mathcal{R} = 2\mathbf{I} \succ \mathbf{0}$. The unique global minimum sits precisely in the unvisited, zero-density void between the two demonstration modes ($p(\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{o}] \mid \mathbf{o}) \approx 0$).

Changing the regression penalty does not by itself represent alternative actions. Mean absolute error ($L_1$) admits conditional medians, while Huber loss limits the influence of large residuals. Neither guarantees a unique, coherent route through a multimodal demonstration distribution. The decoder must represent the alternatives, and execution must maintain a consistent choice across successive observations.

Several decoder families represent these alternatives at different computational costs. **Mixture Density Networks (MDNs)** parameterize a Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM): $p(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o}) = \sum_{m=1}^M \pi_m(\mathbf{o}) \mathcal{N}\left(\mathbf{a} \mid \boldsymbol{\mu}_m(\mathbf{o}), \boldsymbol{\Sigma}_m(\mathbf{o})\right)$. They produce mixture parameters in one forward pass, but training must prevent covariance collapse ($\sigma_m^2 \to 0$) and loss of less frequent modes. The component count and covariance representation become consequential for high-dimensional chunks ($D = d_a \times H$).

With **Energy-Based Models (EBMs)**, a scalar energy scores each candidate: $p(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o}) \propto \exp(-E_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{a}))$. Selecting a low-energy action requires a search whose iteration budget, convergence, and latency must fit the proposal deadline. The choice is therefore between an explicit distribution whose complexity is fixed in the head and an implicit distribution whose candidates require optimization.

Generative architectures, including diffusion models and flow matching, offer another way to represent $p(\mathbf{a} \mid \mathbf{o})$. They train a model to refine a noisy action candidate toward the learned distribution rather than returning its conditional mean. Sampling can then select a coherent demonstration mode ($\mathbf{a}_{\text{left}}$ or $\mathbf{a}_{\text{right}}$). Representing multiple modes addresses the averaging problem, but a generated candidate can still violate clearance or actuator constraints. The permission path must check it before execution.

A mode boundary in a single-step Markov policy can also produce high-frequency temporal chattering. In a $50\text{--}100\text{ Hz}$ feedback loop, microscopic sensor noise drives consecutive observations back and forth across the mode boundary, causing a single-step controller mapping $\mathbf{o}_t \to \mathbf{a}_t$ to alternate between opposing actuator efforts (e.g., $+10\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ and $-10\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$). This alternation excites drivetrain resonances, accelerates gear tooth fatigue, and drives motor winding temperatures toward their thermal limit.

### Compounding errors and recovery experience {#sec-training-recovery-experience-6a31}

A policy can choose a coherent route around the column and still drift into states its demonstrations never covered. Mode averaging concerns the action selected at one observation; compounding error concerns the observations created by successive actions. Keeping these failures separate prevents a richer action decoder from being mistaken for recovery experience. Here $\mathbf{s}$ denotes physical state, $\pi^*$ the expert, and $d^{\pi^*}(\mathbf{s})$ the distribution of states the expert visits. Behavioral cloning minimizes the action mismatch $\ell$ over those recorded states:
$$\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s} \sim d^{\pi^*}} \left[ \ell\left(\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{s}), \pi^*(\mathbf{s})\right) \right].$$
The fixed archive supplies the states used by the loss. Deployment instead follows $\mathbf{s}_{t+1} \sim P(\mathbf{s}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)$, where $P$ describes how the next state depends on the current state and action. Online reinforcement learning can sample that feedback under its current policy, whose visited-state distribution is $d^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\mathbf{s})$. Its objective $J$ is expected accumulated reward $r$, with discount factor $\gamma$ weighting later rewards over horizon $T$:
$$\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J(\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s}_t \sim d^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}, \mathbf{a}_t \sim \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^T \gamma^t r(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t) \right],$$
Fixed-archive BC does not itself collect the states created by its own execution errors. In continuous physical state spaces, this structural decoupling triggers **compounding covariate shift** under Principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift}.

The physical effect of persistent action error depends on what the action commands. Let $\epsilon = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s} \sim d^{\pi^*}}\left[\|\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{s}) - \pi^*(\mathbf{s})\|\right]$ denote the average single-step policy error evaluated under the demonstration distribution. The calculations below illustrate errors that persist without corrective feedback, with fixed control intervals and bounded dynamic coefficients. They sum physical displacement over time; they are not a derivation of the worst-case imitation-learning cost bound. The distinction matters because displacement, accumulated task cost, and probability of collision are different quantities. Persistent velocity errors integrate differently from persistent torque errors:

1. **Kinematic Control (Velocity Tracking):** When actions command velocities ($\dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{v}$), a single-step action error $\Delta \mathbf{a}_t \sim \mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$ manifests as an uncorrected velocity discrepancy $\Delta \mathbf{v}_t \sim \mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$. Integrating this discrepancy over control interval $\Delta t$ shifts the physical state by $\Delta \mathbf{s}_t \approx \sum_{k=1}^t \Delta \mathbf{v}_k \Delta t \sim \mathcal{O}(t \epsilon)$. Integrating this displacement over an entire execution horizon of $T$ control steps yields cumulative trajectory drift:
   $$\text{Cumulative Drift} = \sum_{t=1}^T \|\mathbf{s}_t - \mathbf{s}_t^*\| \approx \sum_{t=1}^T \mathcal{O}(t \epsilon) = \mathcal{O}\left(T^2 \epsilon\right).$$
2. **Dynamic Control (Direct Torque and Current Control):** When actions command generalized actuator torques ($\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q})\ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{h} = \boldsymbol{\tau}$), a single-step error manifests as an uncorrected acceleration discrepancy $\Delta \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_t = \mathbf{M}^{-1}\Delta \boldsymbol{\tau}_t \sim \mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$. Second-order Newtonian integration double-integrates this acceleration error into velocity error $\Delta \dot{\mathbf{q}}_t \sim \mathcal{O}(t \epsilon)$ and position displacement $\Delta \mathbf{q}_t \sim \mathcal{O}(t^2 \epsilon)$. Over an uncorrected execution horizon $T$, cumulative trajectory drift compounds cubically as $\sum_{t=1}^T \mathcal{O}(t^2 \epsilon) = \mathcal{O}(T^3 \epsilon)$ unless actively arrested by a low-level physical feedback controller.

These examples explain why the control interface and the available feedback matter when interpreting an action error. The worst-case imitation-learning cost can grow as $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ under the assumptions of the corresponding bound, but that scaling alone specifies neither a collision time nor a physical displacement. Offline validation on demonstration splits measures prediction accuracy on the demonstrated distribution; recovery after displacement requires additional closed-loop evidence.

Interactive imitation learning methods such as **Dataset Aggregation (DAgger)** [@ross2011reduction] obtain expert labels during learner-generated execution. At iteration $k$, the learner samples states $\mathbf{s} \sim d^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}$, queries an expert $\pi^*$ for labels, appends the new state-action pairs to the dataset $\mathcal{D} \leftarrow \mathcal{D} \cup \{(\mathbf{s}, \pi^*(\mathbf{s}))\}$, and retrains. Aggregating learner-visited states across $\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K d^{\pi_k}$ addresses the mismatch between demonstration and execution distributions. The linear cost scaling $\mathcal{O}(T \epsilon)$ requires the learning and reduction assumptions of the analysis; it does not assert that an expert can recover every physical state.

On hardware, collecting those labels requires a recoverable rollout and an expert who has enough information to choose a correction. A camera log may support a path label while leaving contact force or joint torque ambiguous. Live supervision supplies richer feedback, but the machine continues moving during human reaction and control handoff. Intervention must begin within the available stopping margin, and the handoff must avoid discontinuous setpoints.

Expert availability also does not imply physical recoverability. The machine may lack enough actuator effort or frictional grip to return from a deviation. In the simplified force balance $\mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{q}} = \boldsymbol{\tau} + \mathbf{J}_c^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda}$, $\mathbf{q}$ denotes joint positions, $\mathbf{M}$ inertia, $\boldsymbol{\tau}$ actuator torque, and $\mathbf{J}_c^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda}$ contact forces mapped into joint torques; other forces are omitted here for clarity. Actuator limits require $|\tau_i| \le \tau_{i,\max}$ for every joint axis $i$, while available friction bounds tangential force by $\|\mathbf{f}_t\| \le \mu f_n$, with normal force $f_n$ and friction coefficient $\mu$. These constraints can leave no action that restores the task. Interactive aggregation is therefore most useful where learner deviations can be contained, labeled, and repeated within the operator-time and hardware-exposure budget. It supplies recovery experience; it cannot make an unrecoverable state recoverable.

For the latch, these distinctions select a concrete next training step. The stipulated follow-up campaign in @sec-data supplies `latch-recovery-02`, a versioned archive of expert recovery from the positively displaced plate at the guarded approach. We train `latch-bc-recovery-02` on the original nominal demonstrations and those attributable corrections. Learner commands that preceded takeover remain failure evidence unless an expert supplied replacement labels; they do not become imitation targets merely because the episode eventually succeeded. A multimodal chunk decoder can preserve a coherent back-off and re-seating sequence, while the additional demonstrations supply the recovery states that changing the decoder alone could not provide.

The training decision is complete, but the improvement claim remains to be tested. Entire collection sessions are held out for nominal and recovery checks, so neighboring frames from one run do not appear on both sides of the split. Training diagnostics check whether the candidate represents the demonstrated correction; qualification must then test whether it completes the door task under the declared perturbation without regressing nominal behavior. The candidate carries that request to @sec-evaluation, including task completion, cycle time, proposer intervention, and protective outcomes as separate measures. This is a stipulated engineering branch, not a report of collected data or measured improvement. The negative displacement and faster approach remain unsupported.

[^fn-math-mode-averaging]: **Mode averaging under L2 loss**\index{Mode averaging!mathematical derivation}: Under an $L_2$ regression loss, expected risk $\mathcal{R}(\hat{a}) = \int \|\hat{a} - a\|_2^2 p(a \mid o) da$ is strictly convex with respect to $\hat{a}$. Differentiating and setting the gradient to zero yields $2 \int (\hat{a} - a) p(a \mid o) da = 0 \implies \hat{a}^* = \mathbb{E}[a \mid o]$. For a nonlinear plant, the state transition $\mathbb{E}[f_{\text{plant}}(a)]$ generally diverges from $f_{\text{plant}}(\mathbb{E}[a])$, meaning the mean action does not produce the mean state. In obstacle avoidance, the conditional mean lies entirely outside the manifold of safe actions.

### Temporal horizon expansion and residual coupling in action chunking {#sec-training-action-chunking}

Action chunking (\ref{dfn-brain-action-chunking}) addresses both high-frequency actuator chattering and mode oscillation by predicting an entire sequence of future actions simultaneously. Rather than regressing a single action $\mathbf{a}_t$ from current observation $\mathbf{o}_t$, a chunking policy predicts a setpoint sequence $\mathbf{A}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times d_a}$ across a prediction horizon of $H$ future timesteps and $d_a$ action dimensions. The execution path must interpolate that sequence into continuous motion and check its feasibility. In supervised behavioral cloning, the policy minimizes a multi-step trajectory loss over demonstrated trajectories:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{chunk}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{o}_t, \mathbf{A}_t^*) \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \sum_{i=0}^{H-1} \ell_\delta\left( \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{o}_t)_i - \mathbf{a}^*_{t+i} \right) \right],$$
where $\mathbf{A}_t^* = [\mathbf{a}_t^*, \dots, \mathbf{a}_{t+H-1}^*]^\top$ represents the recorded demonstration chunk, $\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{o}_t)_i$ is the $i$-th predicted future setpoint, and $\ell_\delta(r)$ is a robust Huber loss penalty:
$$\ell_\delta(r) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} r^2 & \text{for } |r| \le \delta, \\ \delta \left(|r| - \frac{1}{2} \delta\right) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
(In latent architectures like ACT [@zhao2023learning], the architecture of both latch policies, this objective is augmented with a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) loss $\beta D_{\text{KL}}(q(\mathbf{z} \mid \mathbf{A}_t^*, \mathbf{o}_t) \parallel p(\mathbf{z}))$ to capture multimodal user intent across demonstrations.)

Teleoperated setpoints can contain outliers caused by tremor, tracking errors, or dropouts. Squared loss gives a large residual disproportionate influence over the fit, whereas a robust loss limits that influence. Neither objective directly constrains the velocity, acceleration, or jerk of the resulting trajectory.

Huber loss transitions from quadratic $L_2$ regression for small errors ($|r| \le \delta$) to robust linear $L_1$ regression for large errors ($|r| > \delta$). Its gradient is strictly bounded:
$$\nabla_r \ell_\delta(r) = \begin{cases} r & \text{for } |r| \le \delta, \\ \delta \operatorname{sgn}(r) & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}$$
For residuals exceeding the threshold $\delta$, the gradient saturates at a constant magnitude $\delta$, limiting each outlier's influence on the fit. The threshold acts on prediction residuals, however, rather than directly on velocity, acceleration, or jerk. Huber loss alone therefore establishes neither smooth motion nor actuator feasibility; those properties need explicit constraints and checks on the proposed chunk.

Predicting $H$ future actions at once creates opportunities for more coherent execution, provided training and runtime checks preserve them:

1. **Temporal and Dynamic Consistency**: Jointly predicting adjacent actions lets the model learn their relationships. The resulting sequence still requires checks for abrupt changes and actuator limits.
2. **Preserving Modal Commitment**: A chunk can represent one coherent choice, such as passing left of the column, across adjacent actions. Predicting a sequence does not itself ensure that the decoder selects a single valid mode.
3. **Receding-Horizon Replanning and Temporal Ensembling**: The deployed policy queries a fresh chunk every $H_a$ steps ($H_a < H$), permitting feedback correction before the prediction horizon ends (@sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline). Blending overlapping predictions is optional and must preserve a coherent mode and feasible seam.

Crucially, receding-horizon temporal ensembling introduces an acute physical failure mode at decision bifurcation points. If the policy queries a fresh trajectory chunk near an obstacle, stochastic generative sampling may select mode A (steer left) at step $t$ and mode B (steer right) at step $t+1$. Exponentially smoothing these overlapping chunks across the receding horizon blends the opposing velocity vectors along the execution seam, resurrecting the exact mode-averaging failure that action chunking was chosen to eliminate.[^fn-ctrl-commitment-horizon]

[^fn-ctrl-commitment-horizon]: **Mode Commitment Horizons in Temporal Ensembling**\index{Action chunking!mode commitment}\index{Temporal ensembling!mode averaging failure}: To prevent receding-horizon temporal ensembling from resurrecting mode averaging near obstacles, production controllers enforce a mode commitment horizon: the controller can retain the selected mode over an execution window rather than smoothing conflicting directions. This commitment never overrides a state limit, evidence expiry, or lease expiry; the qualified fallback takes precedence when continued execution is invalid.

Chunking changes how often the policy replans, but does not supply recovery states absent from the demonstrations. Executing $H_a$ actions between queries reduces the number of query boundaries to $T_{\text{eff}} = T/H_a$ while leaving disturbances within each execution window to the lower-level feedback system. This count alone does not convert the imitation-learning cost bound $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$ into a task-survival curve. ACT [@zhao2023learning] and receding-horizon diffusion [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] change temporal execution; DAgger [@ross2011reduction] changes the training distribution by obtaining labels on learner-visited states. These are separate ways to improve behavior, and their closed-loop benefits must be measured on the task. The normalized displacement sketches in @fig-06-compounding-error retain the persistent-error assumptions of the earlier calculation. Neither those sketches nor the imitation-learning cost bound establishes a task-survival probability or ranks learning algorithms.

::: {#fig-06-compounding-error fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Horizon dependence under persistent error**: Dimensionless sketches of the quadratic and cubic cumulative-displacement relationships derived above, normalized to agree at a reference horizon. The curves assume persistent error without corrective feedback and fixed dynamic coefficients. They illustrate growth rates, not measured task survival, collision probability, or a ranking of learning algorithms." fig-alt="Two increasing curves of normalized cumulative displacement against normalized execution horizon. The cubic relationship rises more steeply than the quadratic relationship after their common reference point. A label identifies both as illustrative growth laws, not task-survival curves."}

```{python}
#| label: fig-06-compounding-error
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NORMALIZED HORIZON DEPENDENCE UNDER PERSISTENT ERROR
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-06-compounding-error follows the displacement examples.
# │ Goal: Separate a growth-law sketch from empirical task-survival evidence.
# │ Show: Quadratic and cubic growth normalized at one reference horizon.
# │ How: Plot the previously derived T^2 and T^3 relationships in dimensionless
# │      reference units; no probabilities or measured outcomes are supplied.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(8, 4.5))
horizon_ratio = np.linspace(1, 4, 200)
ax.plot(horizon_ratio, horizon_ratio**2, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], linewidth=2.2, label=r"Quadratic growth: $(T/T_0)^2$")
ax.plot(horizon_ratio, horizon_ratio**3, color=COLORS["OrangeLine"], linewidth=2.2, linestyle="--", label=r"Cubic growth: $(T/T_0)^3$")
ax.set_xlabel(r"Execution horizon / reference horizon, $T/T_0$")
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative displacement / reference value")
ax.set_xlim(0.9, 4.1)
ax.set_ylim(0, 70)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", frameon=True)
ax.text(0.04, 0.60, "Illustrative growth laws\nNo task-survival probability implied", transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10, va="top")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()
```
:::

Increasing dataset size, model capacity, or tuning can reduce the one-step error rate on evaluated observations and therefore lower the chance of a first policy error during a fixed horizon. That improvement does not characterize what happens after an error. An external disturbance, uncalibrated payload, or voltage sag can also move the machine into weakly supported states without a policy disagreement. Recovery data, measured dynamics, and independent runtime limits determine whether either event remains within the physical envelope.

Drift off the demonstrated states raises no alarm of its own, so detecting it before physical contact cannot rely on the offline training loss. A feature-distance or uncertainty monitor can flag unfamiliar observations, but its threshold needs validation against missed detections and false alarms. For the latch, an independently measured plate position and approach condition provide a more direct check of the declared cells. A convex hull around demonstrations does not certify that all states inside it support the task.

### Runtime computational overhead of policy decoder architectures {#sec-training-decoder-costs}

Selecting a coherent route does not ensure that the robot receives its next proposal in time. A decoder converts the model's representation into an action or action sequence; iterative decoders repeatedly refine a candidate before returning it. Their equations describe how a candidate is generated, while the execution decision depends on the time those dependent model evaluations consume. The central comparison is between measured proposal latency and the deadline of the buffer that feeds the permission path.

The same multimodal choice now has a computational cost. @Fig-06-diffusion-denoising contrasts direct regression with iterative trajectory sampling and shows how chunk buffering separates that sampling from actuator playback.

::: {#fig-06-diffusion-denoising fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Generative policy architectures and action chunk denoising**: (a) Sampling represents alternative demonstrated routes instead of their direct-regression mean. (b) Iterative refinement produces a candidate action chunk whose clearance and actuator feasibility still require checking. (c) A schematic dual-rate arrangement buffers host proposals for a faster execution path. The labeled rates illustrate the arrangement, not a qualified latch timing contract; buffering alone guarantees neither freshness nor freedom from starvation." fig-alt="Three-panel diagram showing generative diffusion policy mechanics. Panel (a) illustrates multimodal resolution, contrasting direct regression mean collision with diffusion mode selection. Panel (b) illustrates iterative denoising from pure noise at Step K down to a smooth action chunk at Step 0. Panel (c) illustrates dual-rate decoupling from host MPU at 15 Hz through a shared ring buffer down to a 1 kHz MCU driving physical actuators."}
![](images/svg/fig06_bespoke_diffusion_denoising_process.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy] learn to remove noise from demonstrated action chunks conditioned on the observation history. At inference, each denoising evaluation consumes the preceding candidate, so the evaluations occur sequentially. Flow matching [@lipman2022flow; @black2024pi0] instead learns a vector field that transports a noisy candidate toward the demonstrated distribution. Its solver also incurs a sequence of model evaluations. Neither construction guarantees collision-free or actuator-feasible output. The diffusion and flow-matching objectives are developed in @sec-appendix-ml-diffusion; for the latch decision, their relevant consequence is how many evaluations yield adequate action quality within the available time.

Autoregressive vision-language-action policies [@kim2024openvla] incur a related dependency by generating successive action tokens. Their cost depends on the tokenization, model, and implementation, rather than on the decoder family name alone. We therefore compare complete proposal latency, including perception, with the actual proposal deadline before selecting the execution arrangement.

The number and dependency of decoder evaluations constrain proposal latency; the implementation and loaded hardware determine its measured value. The total wall-clock duration of a single policy inference cycle $t_{\text{infer}}$ is the sum of perceptual feature extraction and iterative generative trajectory sampling:
$$t_{\text{infer}} = t_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf{O}_t) + \sum_{k=1}^K t_{\text{step}}\left(\mathbf{A}^k, k\right) \le t_{\text{deadline}},$$
where $t_{\text{enc}}$ is the visual backbone and proprioceptive encoding latency, $K$ is the number of denoising or ODE solver integration steps, $t_{\text{step}}$ is the per-step neural forward pass latency of the action head, and $t_{\text{deadline}}$ is the real-time execution deadline.

The encoder runs once per proposal, whereas each dependent decoder evaluation adds work. The memory-wall analysis of @sec-brain-memory-wall explains why repeatedly fetching a large action head can dominate that work. The relevant arithmetic intensity depends on the architecture and reuse within each evaluation; batch size alone does not establish that all policy decoders have the same bottleneck.

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-decoder-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DECODER BUDGET: THE DEPLOYED ACT DECODER VERSUS A 16-STEP DIFFUSION HEAD
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-training-decoder-costs and the latch policy manifest.
# │ Goal: Price an iterative diffusion head that could replace the one-pass
# │       ACT decoder of latch-bc-01 against the machine's setpoint step,
# │       renewal period, and the lease rule's jitter allowance.
# │ Show: 2.4 GB of head traffic, >= 11.8 ms at the 204 GB/s peak; 48 ms
# │       stipulated DDIM latency and 2.5 ms per evaluation; 18 ms for four
# │       flow evaluations; 2 ms of renewal slack against ACT's 10 ms; a 5 ms
# │       stretch carries the diffusion head 3 ms past its renewal.
# │ How: D = K x M; t_mem = D / B_peak; t_eval = (t_infer - t_enc) / K;
# │      deployed decoder and periods from RM (2026-09-28, M5).
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_display_math

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class DecoderBudget:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    act_params = RM.chunk_model.parameters  # category: datasheet (ACT, the deployed chunk policy)
    horizon = RM.chunk_horizon  # category: chosen (setpoints per chunk)
    t_act = RM.chunk_inference_latency.to(millisecond)  # category: illustrative (P99 incl. vision)
    t_step = RM.chunk_step.to(millisecond)  # category: chosen (setpoint step, synchronous deadline)
    t_renew = RM.chunk_period  # category: derived (renewal period, asynchronous deadline)
    b_peak = RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth  # category: datasheet (application-processor peak)
    m_head = 150 * MB  # category: illustrative (diffusion action-head weights)
    k_ddim = 16  # category: illustrative (DDIM denoising steps)
    k_flow = 4  # category: illustrative (flow-matching evaluations)
    t_enc = 8 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (visual encoding, once per proposal)
    t_ddim = 48 * millisecond  # category: illustrative (stipulated total DDIM inference)
    t_jitter = 5 * millisecond  # category: chosen (renewal-jitter allowance of the lease rule, @sec-nervous-coupled-budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    d_mem = (k_ddim * m_head).to(GB)
    t_mem = (d_mem / b_peak).to(millisecond)
    t_eval = ((t_ddim - t_enc) / k_ddim).to(millisecond)
    t_flow = (t_enc + k_flow * t_eval).to(millisecond)
    slack_act = (t_renew - t_act).to(millisecond)
    slack_ddim = (t_renew - t_ddim).to(millisecond)
    ddim_stretch_over = (t_ddim + t_jitter - t_renew).to(millisecond)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(d_mem.magnitude - 2.4) < 1e-9, f"head traffic {d_mem}")
    check(abs(t_mem.magnitude - 11.765) < 1e-3, f"transfer floor {t_mem}")
    check(abs(t_eval.magnitude - 2.5) < 1e-9, f"per-evaluation time {t_eval}")
    check(abs(t_flow.magnitude - 18.0) < 1e-9, f"flow latency {t_flow}")
    check(t_ddim > t_step, "DDIM must overrun the synchronous setpoint deadline")
    check(t_flow < t_step, "four flow evaluations must fit the synchronous setpoint deadline")
    check(t_mem < t_ddim, "the transfer floor must sit below the stipulated latency")
    check(t_act < t_ddim < t_renew, "both decoders must fit the renewal period, ACT with more slack")
    check(abs(slack_act.magnitude - 10.0) < 1e-9 and abs(slack_ddim.magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "renewal slack")
    check(t_act + t_jitter < t_renew, "a jitter-sized stretch must leave ACT inside its renewal period")
    check(abs(ddim_stretch_over.magnitude - 3.0) < 1e-9, f"diffusion overrun under stretch {ddim_stretch_over}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    act_params_str = fmt_params(act_params, precision=0)
    horizon_str = fmt_int(horizon)
    t_act_str = fmt_latency(t_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    m_head_str = fmt_memory(m_head, unit=MB, precision=0)
    k_ddim_str = fmt_int(k_ddim)
    k_flow_str = fmt_int(k_flow)
    b_peak_str = fmt_bandwidth(b_peak, unit=GB / second, precision=0)
    t_enc_str = fmt_latency(t_enc, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_ddim_str = fmt_latency(t_ddim, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_eval_str = fmt_latency(t_eval, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_flow_str = fmt_latency(t_flow, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    slack_act_str = fmt_latency(slack_act, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    slack_ddim_str = fmt_latency(slack_ddim, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    ddim_stretch_over_str = fmt_latency(ddim_stretch_over, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    d_mem_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"D_{{\text{{mem}}}} = {k_ddim_str} \times {fmt(m_head.to(MB).magnitude, precision=0)}\,\text{{MB}} = {fmt(d_mem.magnitude, precision=1)}\,\text{{GB}}."
    )
    t_mem_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"t_{{\text{{mem}}}} \ge \frac{{D_{{\text{{mem}}}}}}{{B_{{\text{{mem}}}}}} = \frac{{{fmt(d_mem.magnitude, precision=1)}\,\text{{GB}}}}{{{fmt(b_peak.to(GB / second).magnitude, precision=0)}\,\text{{GB/s}}}} \approx {fmt(t_mem.magnitude, precision=1)}\,\text{{ms}},"
    )
```

For an action head parameterized by $M$ weight bytes, suppose the weights do not remain in cache between evaluations. A streaming estimate then charges one weight fetch per evaluation:
$$D_{\text{mem}} = K \times M.$$
The latch policies do not pay this cost: `latch-bc-01` decodes each chunk with the machine's `{python} DecoderBudget.act_params_str`-parameter ACT network in one pass, within the `{python} DecoderBudget.t_act_str` P99 inference target of @sec-brain. Consider instead replacing its decoder with an illustrative diffusion head of $M =$ `{python} DecoderBudget.m_head_str` operating under a $K =$ `{python} DecoderBudget.k_ddim_str` step DDIM schedule. The total DRAM traffic per inference cycle reaches:
`{python} DecoderBudget.d_mem_math`
At the application processor's peak unified memory bandwidth, $B_{\text{mem}} =$ `{python} DecoderBudget.b_peak_str`, memory transfer alone consumes:
`{python} DecoderBudget.t_mem_math`
a lower bound that does not determine the full execution time. Arithmetic can overlap memory transfers, while kernel launch, synchronization, and feature processing can add costs; they require an implementation-specific timing model. The bandwidth estimate is not a latency measurement. Stipulate a visual encoding latency of $t_{\text{enc}} =$ `{python} DecoderBudget.t_enc_str` and a total inference duration $t_{\text{infer}} \approx$ `{python} DecoderBudget.t_ddim_str` once all evaluation work is included, which leaves `{python} DecoderBudget.t_eval_str` per denoising evaluation; these inputs define the comparison below.

The illustrative budget distinguishes sampler choice from execution authority:

1. **Synchronous setpoint deadline:** The stipulated DDIM latency exceeds the next `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str` setpoint tick, so it cannot supply every tick synchronously. A compact `{python} DecoderBudget.k_flow_str`-evaluation flow-matching candidate, at `{python} DecoderBudget.t_enc_str` of encoding plus `{python} DecoderBudget.k_flow_str` evaluations of `{python} DecoderBudget.t_eval_str`, needs `{python} DecoderBudget.t_flow_str` and fits the compute-only budget. It becomes a viable synchronous choice only if action quality, scheduling, transfer, and admission also fit. A faster decoder does not remove the permission check.
2. **Number of function evaluations:** A higher-order solver can use fewer integration steps while performing more network evaluations. Standard RK4 evaluates four stages per step; compare that total work with the single-stage alternative before choosing it. Distillation or a different solver is useful when it reduces measured latency without losing the recovery behavior the latch needs.
3. **Asynchronous proposal renewal:** The slower candidate can instead generate chunks against the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str` renewal cadence while the execution path plays an admitted prefix. There its margin is thin. The diffusion head leaves `{python} DecoderBudget.slack_ddim_str` of the renewal period, where the deployed ACT decoder leaves `{python} DecoderBudget.slack_act_str`. A contention stretch the size of the lease rule's `{python} DecoderBudget.t_jitter_str` renewal-jitter allowance (@sec-nervous-coupled-budget) leaves ACT inside its period but carries the diffusion head `{python} DecoderBudget.ddim_stretch_over_str` past it, so every such renewal would draw on the allowance that transport, validation, and mailbox delays also need. This compute-only fit still needs loaded timing evidence. The prediction horizon supplies candidate motion; it does not authorize playback for the entire horizon. The lease selected in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing bounds active permission separately from renewal cadence and evidence age. Fresh evidence and a valid replacement can renew execution; a new header cannot renew stale observations. An invalid new proposal leaves a valid active prefix in place only while that prefix's own state, evidence, and lease remain valid. On expiry, the execution path invokes a state-dependent, physically qualified fallback. Powered deceleration requires drive energy; a holding brake is engaged according to its qualified sequence, not credited with an unspecified emergency stop.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Hardware placement of multi-rate action chunk buffers across the application processor and the safety microcontroller is engineered in @sec-placement-two-paths-one-die.
:::

### Offline reinforcement learning and action distributional shift {#sec-training-offline-rl}

When physical demonstration datasets $\mathcal{D} = \{(s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1})\}$ contain heterogeneous or sub-optimal trajectories (e.g., mixtures of teleoperation, scripted routines, and exploratory human play), behavioral cloning struggles because it treats all demonstrations with equal supervised weight. In classical reinforcement learning formulated on Markov decision processes (MDPs) [@sutton2018reinforcement], an agent optimizes a policy to maximize expected discounted cumulative returns $J = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=0}^\infty \gamma^t r(s_t, a_t)\right]$. **Offline reinforcement learning (Batch RL)**\index{Offline reinforcement learning} aims to optimize a policy directly from logged transition archives without active hardware exploration, using reward signals to stitch together high-performing composite trajectories from disjoint, imperfect demonstrations [@kumar2020conservative].

However, applying standard Q-learning to static offline datasets triggers a failure mode known as **out-of-distribution (OOD) action overestimation**\index{Out-of-distribution action overestimation}. In standard reinforcement learning, the algorithm estimates the value of future states by asking its value network to predict the highest possible return it could achieve from the next step (for formal Bellman equations, see @sec-appendix-ml-affordances). That maximum is taken over the entire continuous action space. For actions that were never executed in the logging dataset, the network has received zero training signal and often outputs erroneously large value estimates due to generalization variance, predicting a high return for an untried physical maneuver. The algorithm greedily selects these spurious peaks, propagating over-optimistic value errors backwards. When deployed, the policy selects these ungrounded actions, and it can command motions that stall a joint or strike a boundary.

The distinction from cloning is the selection rule $\pi(\mathbf{s}) = \arg\max_{\mathbf{a}} Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a})$. Maximization can favor an unsupported action precisely because its estimated value is too high. Offline learning therefore needs a way to limit optimism without obtaining new transitions from the machine.

To reduce value overestimation without querying the physical environment, **Conservative Q-learning (CQL)**\index{Conservative Q-Learning} adds a conservative penalty to value fitting [@kumar2020conservative]. The objective below has two parts: the bracketed term discourages optimism about unsupported actions, and the squared term fits the reward observed in logged transitions together with estimated future reward. Here $\mathcal{A}$ is the action space, $Q$ the value function being fitted, $\hat{Q}$ a fixed target estimate during this update, and $\alpha$ the penalty weight:
$$\min_Q \alpha \cdot \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{s} \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \ln \int_{\mathcal{A}} \exp(Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}))\,d\mathbf{a} - \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a} \sim \mathcal{D}}\left[ Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) \right] \right] + \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}, r, \mathbf{s}') \sim \mathcal{D}} \left[ \left( Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) - \mathcal{B}^* \hat{Q}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) \right)^2 \right],$$
where $\mathcal{B}^* \hat{Q}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = r(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) + \gamma \max_{\mathbf{a}'} \hat{Q}(\mathbf{s}', \mathbf{a}')$ is the empirical Bellman target operator and $\alpha > 0$ balances value conservatism against Bellman error minimization.[^fn-math-cql-bound]

The objective discourages optimistic values for poorly supported actions. In the expression, $Q$ estimates future reward from an action, and the Bellman target combines the immediate reward with the estimated reward that follows. The conservative penalty changes those estimates; it does not impose a hard boundary on executable actions:

1. The logarithmic integral term $\ln \int_{\mathcal{A}} \exp(Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}))\,d\mathbf{a}$ acts as a soft-maximum that actively pushes *down* on Q-values across the entire action space, aggressively depressing values in unvisited action regions where function approximation variance would otherwise create spurious positive spikes.
2. The dataset expectation $\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{a} \sim \mathcal{D}}[Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a})]$ pushes *up* on Q-values exclusively for state-action pairs executed during the logging campaign.
3. When $\alpha = 0$, the conservative penalty disappears and policy extraction uses $\arg\max_{\mathbf{a}} Q(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a})$ without that correction. With $\alpha > 0$, unsupported actions face a value penalty, but they are not categorically excluded. Physical action limits and checks of operating conditions remain obligations of the independent permission path.

[^fn-math-cql-bound]: **Scope of the CQL bound**\index{Conservative Q-Learning}: Under its data-coverage, optimization, and function-approximation assumptions, CQL constructs a conservative estimate whose *expected value for a policy* lower-bounds that policy's true value [@kumar2020conservative]. This is not a pointwise bound for every state-action pair or every dataset, and expected return does not certify physical safety.

Cloning, chunking, and offline value learning can all propose actions beyond the logged experience. Their training data do not supply evidence for those proposals merely because an optimizer assigns them a low loss or high value. When the archive lacks the recovery maneuvers the task requires, additional experience and validation are needed; closed-loop trial is one way to obtain them.

## Reinforcement Learning and Environment Interaction {#sec-training-learning-by-trial}

The recovery-imitation choice depends on an expert who can supply the missing correction. When expert labels are unavailable or the task requires discovering a new behavior, learning by trial offers a different source of experience. It lets the policy generate trajectories in closed loop and observe the consequences of attempted corrections. In online policy search, the agent updates parameters from the scalar advantage estimates its own rollouts accumulate:
$$\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} J(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\tau)} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^T \nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \ln \pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{a}_t \mid \mathbf{s}_t) \hat{A}_t \right],$$
where $\hat{A}_t = Q(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t) - V(\mathbf{s}_t)$ measures whether an exploratory action performed better or worse than the baseline expectation. Transitions come from the state occupancy distribution $d^{\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}}(\mathbf{s})$ induced by the active policy weights. A rollout can therefore expose the learner to its own deviations and supply feedback on attempted recovery. Positive advantage ($\hat{A}_t > 0$) favors an action relative to the estimated baseline; negative advantage ($\hat{A}_t < 0$) discourages it. The reward and observations must make the relevant failure visible for that feedback to be useful. Learning from policy-generated states addresses the mismatch between expert and learner experience, but does not eliminate distribution shift under new disturbances, environments, or hardware dynamics.

On hardware, that experience generates winding heat ($E_{\text{thermal}} = \int I(t)^2 R\,dt$), accumulates mechanical load cycles, and consumes calendar time for execution and reset. The feasible training budget must include these physical costs alongside compute. A method that needs fewer interactions can be preferable even if each parameter update costs more computation.

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-trial-wall-clock
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HARDWARE TRIAL WALL-CLOCK TIME FOR THE LATCH TASK
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The Learning by Trial paragraphs that follow.
# │ Goal: Show that calendar time for on-hardware RL is set by trial count,
# │       rollout length, reset time, and parallelism, and that manual resets
# │       dominate.
# │ Show: rollout time, trial count, automated and manual reset times, and the
# │       resulting single-machine wall-clock durations.
# │ How: T_wall = N (t_rollout + t_reset) / P; all inputs are scenario
# │      assumptions for an illustrative campaign.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_sci

class TrialWallClock:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_rollout = 8.0 * second  # category: illustrative (autonomous contact phase of one opening, not the 25 s collection attempt of @sec-data)
    n_trials = 1_000_000  # category: illustrative (order-of-magnitude trial count)
    p_rigs = 1  # category: illustrative (single physical machine)
    t_reset_auto = 4.0 * second  # category: illustrative (dedicated RL fixture, faster than the 15 s collection re-latch of @sec-data)
    t_reset_manual = 30.0 * second  # category: illustrative (manual operator reset)
    n_reversals_per_trial = 4  # category: illustrative (joint load reversals per opening)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    t_exec = (n_trials * t_rollout / p_rigs).to(second)
    t_auto = (n_trials * (t_rollout + t_reset_auto) / p_rigs).to(second)
    t_manual = (n_trials * (t_rollout + t_reset_manual) / p_rigs).to(second)
    n_reversals = n_trials * n_reversals_per_trial

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_exec.to(day).magnitude - 92.59) < 0.01, f"execution time {t_exec.to(day)}")
    check(abs(t_auto.to(day).magnitude - 138.89) < 0.01, f"automated-reset time {t_auto.to(day)}")
    check(abs(t_manual.to(day).magnitude - 439.81) < 0.01, f"manual-reset time {t_manual.to(day)}")
    check(t_manual > 3 * t_auto, "manual resets must dominate the calendar")
    check(n_reversals == 4_000_000, f"load reversals {n_reversals}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_rollout_str = fmt_time(t_rollout, second, precision=0)
    t_reset_auto_str = fmt_time(t_reset_auto, second, precision=0)
    t_reset_manual_str = fmt_time(t_reset_manual, second, precision=0)
    t_exec_s_str = fmt_sci_qty(t_exec, second, precision=1)
    t_auto_s_str = fmt_sci_qty(t_auto, second, precision=1)
    t_exec_days_str = fmt_time(t_exec, day, precision=1, style="word")
    t_auto_days_str = fmt_time(t_auto, day, precision=1, style="word")
    t_manual_days_str = fmt_time(t_manual, day, precision=1, style="word")
    n_reversals_str = fmt_sci(n_reversals, precision=1)
```

Closed-loop exploration on hardware is billed first in calendar time, which depends on how many trials the algorithm needs, how long each trial lasts, how long a reset takes, and how many machines run in parallel. Consider the door-opening task itself, in which the arm regulates contact forces over an active horizon of $t_{\text{rollout}}$ = `{python} TrialWallClock.t_rollout_str`, the autonomous contact phase of an opening rather than a full teleoperated attempt. Reinforcement learning on high-dimensional sensory inputs can require on the order of $N = 10^6$ trials to discover coordinated force-velocity profiles, the scale of the grasping campaign in @fig-06-robot-arm-farm. On a single physical machine with $P = 1$, the raw execution time alone accounts for `{python} TrialWallClock.t_exec_s_str`, roughly `{python} TrialWallClock.t_exec_days_str` of uninterrupted round-the-clock operation before accounting for any reset overhead.

Factoring in the reset phase reveals the true temporal bottleneck of physical experimentation. If a dedicated automated fixture, faster than the collection rig's re-latch (@sec-data-teleop-costs), re-latches the door and returns the arm to its starting pose in $t_{\text{reset,auto}}$ = `{python} TrialWallClock.t_reset_auto_str`, the total collection time for one million trials expands to `{python} TrialWallClock.t_auto_s_str`, or `{python} TrialWallClock.t_auto_days_str`. When exploratory trajectories jam the latch cam or trigger joint overcurrent trips, automated resetting becomes impossible, requiring a human operator to free the latch, re-seat the door, and re-index the arm. If every trial instead needs a manual reset averaging $t_{\text{reset,manual}}$ = `{python} TrialWallClock.t_reset_manual_str`, the wall-clock requirement grows to `{python} TrialWallClock.t_manual_days_str`. Scaling physical parallelism to clusters of $P = 14$ synchronized rigs (@fig-06-robot-arm-farm) compresses calendar duration to several weeks [@levine2018learning], but it multiplies the physical footprint, capital investment, electrical power delivery, and human supervisory labor proportionally.

::: {#fig-06-robot-arm-farm fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Physical policy training farm**: Fourteen manipulators collecting over 800,000 physical grasp attempts across months [@levine2018learning]. Hardware parallelism divides calendar time but not cost, since each station adds capital, gearbox and bearing wear, thermal load in the motor windings, and a share of the supervisory labor needed to clear dropped objects and jams. Attribution: @levine2018learning." fig-alt="Physical Policy Training Farm and Hardware Parallelism. Large-scale robotic data collection cluster comprising 14 custom articulated manipulators operating concurrently over months to collect over 800,000 physical grasp attempts for vision-based hand-eye coordination [@levine2018learning]. Each robotic station consists of a 7-DoF arm, a two-finger compliant gripper, an over-the-shoulder RGB camera, and a dedicated bin containing diverse household objects. Scaling hardware parallelism to P=14 compresses the wall-clock calendar time Twall = N(trollout + treset)/P, but incurs heavy capital expenditure, continuous mechanical wear across gearboxes and linkage bearings, thermal buildup in motor windings, and substantial supervisory overhead to clear dropped objects and mechanical jams. Attribution: @levine2018learning."}
![](images/png/fig06_real_robot_arm_farm.png){width="85%"}
:::

Time is often not the binding constraint; wear is. Each door opening loads each actuator joint through about $n_{\text{rev}} = 4$ bidirectional load reversals, so $N = 10^6$ trials accumulate `{python} TrialWallClock.n_reversals_str` of them in the drivetrain.[^fn-hw-bearing-life] The same million contact events wear the latch cam and strike plate, crush the gripper's compliant pads, and cycle the harness wiring toward fatigue fracture.

[^fn-hw-bearing-life]: **Bearing life vs. command reversals**\index{Hardware wear!bearing life}: ISO 281 estimates rolling-bearing fatigue life under specified load and speed. A gear-unit catalog may express its wave-generator-bearing $L_{10}$ in operating hours at rated conditions; neither figure converts commanded reversals into consumed gearheads without a unit-specific duty-cycle model.

In a purely computational environment, an exploratory branch that goes numerically unstable costs nothing beyond a discarded buffer. On the running machine, exploration is irreversible. Unconstrained exploratory torque drives mechanisms into rigid fixtures, strips harmonic drive teeth\index{Harmonic drive!fatigue life under RL exploration}, and heats motor stators past their $155^\circ\text{C}$ Class F insulation threshold.[^fn-hw-thermal-insulation]

[^fn-hw-thermal-insulation]: **Winding temperature limit**: @Sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles gives the IEC 60085 Class F rating behind this threshold. Bang-bang torque commands from unregularized reward functions can hold the current high enough to age the insulation quickly.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Motor winding thermal limits and torque-speed derating curves are derived in @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles.
:::

Furthermore, physical degradation alters the plant during the training process itself\index{Plant mutation during training}. In standard Markov Decision Processes, the transition probability kernel $p(\mathbf{s}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)$ is assumed to be strictly stationary. On physical hardware, this assumption fails. As contact surfaces burnish, transmission backlash expands, and mechanical fasteners loosen under repetitive cyclic vibration, the physical transition distribution $p_{n = 900{,}000}(\mathbf{s}_{t+1} \mid \mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t)$ differs measurably from the pristine dynamics at trial $n = 1$. The physical plant mutates under the energetic cost of collecting its own training data, confronting the optimizer with a moving, non-stationary target.

The reward function can also favor physically undesirable behavior\index{Reward hacking}. In trial-based learning, the scalar reward $r(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a})$ specifies what the optimizer values, while the action space, controller, and independent limits constrain what it can do. If neither the reward nor those constraints account for contact force, torque changes, or heating, a high-return policy can exploit that omission. A regularized reward can discourage such behavior:
$$r_{\text{total}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) = r_{\text{task}}(\mathbf{s}, \mathbf{a}) - \lambda_{\tau} \|\boldsymbol{\tau}_t\|_2^2 - \lambda_{\dot{\tau}} \left\| \frac{\boldsymbol{\tau}_t - \boldsymbol{\tau}_{t-1}}{\Delta t} \right\|_2^2 - \lambda_T \max\left(0, T_{\text{motor}} - T_{\text{thresh}}\right).$$
For example, a tracking-only reward can favor rapid switching between current limits when the action space and lower-level controller permit it. Such switching can excite mechanical vibration and increase thermal load. Unpenalized contact can likewise favor bracing against a stop if that improves the score and no independent limit prevents it. These are possible optimizer outcomes, not inevitable consequences of omitting a particular reward term. The penalty weights above trade task progress against effort, torque slew, and temperature; finite penalties still do not establish hard physical limits.

For low-dimensional systems with trivial resets, negligible wear, and wide safety margins, reinforcement learning directly on hardware remains viable. When the projected interaction budget exceeds the apparatus's calendar, wear, or thermal limits, simulation can supply additional exploratory experience. The alternative may be a more sample-efficient method, better demonstrations, or a narrower task. For the simulated route, parallel rollout capacity must be assessed together with the model's physical fidelity.

This substitution fundamentally alters the contract between training and reality. A policy trained inside a virtual environment bends no mechanical linkages during exploration. However, it inherits every omission of the reward function and every numerical approximation of the physics solver. A policy can learn to depend on a relaxed contact constraint or an omitted delay. Such dependencies can become control failures on hardware, so transfer evidence must test the mechanisms relevant to the chosen task.

## The Simulator as a System Component {#sec-training-simulator-component}

The latch policy learned that a fast plunge was acceptable because its simulated plate yielded more than the physical plate. Removing the simulator at deployment does not remove that learned behavior. A simulator therefore belongs in the training system's engineering specification: its equations, contact approximations, and timing assumptions determine the experience supplied to the optimizer. The engineer needs measurable error tolerances for those assumptions before using simulated success as evidence about the machine.

::: {#dfn-training-sim-real-reality-gap-vector .callout-definition title="Sim-to-real reality gap vector"}

***Sim-to-real reality gap vector***\index{Sim-to-real reality gap vector!definition}\index{Reality gap!definition} $\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{\text{sim2real}} = [\Delta_{\text{dyn}}, \Delta_{\text{sens}}, \Delta_{\text{vis}}, \Delta_{\text{lat}}]$ is the coupled, multi-channel decomposition of physical discrepancies between simulated and hardware environments spanning contact mechanics ($\Delta_{\text{dyn}}$), sensor transduction and noise ($\Delta_{\text{sens}}$), visual appearance ($\Delta_{\text{vis}}$), and asynchronous transport latency and jitter ($\Delta_{\text{lat}}$).

1.  **Significance**: Treating the "reality gap" as a scalar difficulty metric or pure visual domain mismatch causes engineers to overlook dynamical and temporal divergences. Discrepancies in actuator back-EMF, gearbox compliance, or bus jitter deplete feedback stability margins before the policy completes its first physical control step.
2.  **Distinction**: An inaccurate parameter value (such as a 10 percent error in link mass) preserves the causal differential equations of motion, whereas an omitted mechanism (such as zero-delay communication or unmodeled Coulomb stick-slip) entirely severs physical feedback paths, leading policies to exploit non-physical simulator artifacts.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Relying exclusively on extreme domain randomization to bridge large gaps. Randomizing parameters across unphysical ranges dilutes policy capacity, resulting in overly conservative, sluggish behaviors that fail to achieve precision tasks on real hardware.

:::

Like any hardware subsystem, the simulator requires a formal interface contract, stated in quantities that can be measured and budgeted. This contract specifies observation dimensions, action bounds, simulation time step $\Delta t$, transport latency between command issuance and physical actuation, actuator torque and current limits, sensor noise distributions, reset distributions, and termination conditions. If the simulator specifies an observation loop executing at $100\text{ Hz}$ with an assumed zero-delay sensor channel and Gaussian noise with variance $\sigma^2 = 1.0 \times 10^{-4}\text{ (rad/s)}^2$, the policy learns feedback gains tuned to those precise signal statistics, and an unmodeled $15\text{ ms}$ bus transport delay on the physical machine invalidates them. Dactyl's twin (@fig-06-sim2real-dactyl) could not match its physical hand exactly, so its simulator was calibrated against the real hand and then randomized around the calibrated values, and the policy met the unmatched remainder as variation it had already trained against [@andrychowicz2020learning].

The interface contract matters more when simulation supplies most of the training experience. The selected throughput scenarios in @fig-06-simulation-scaling illustrate the scale of rollout budgets that motivates parallel execution, without establishing a benchmark ranking.

::: {#fig-06-sim2real-dactyl fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Sim-to-real transfer setup**: OpenAI's Dactyl apparatus, a 24-DoF Shadow Hand inside a motion-capture cage beside the MuJoCo digital twin it was trained in [@andrychowicz2020learning]. Transfer is bought with domain randomization over friction, damping, actuator gains, masses, dimensions, and lighting, together with modeled backlash and action delay, which works by forcing the policy to treat unmodeled physical variation as noise rather than by making the simulator accurate. Attribution: @andrychowicz2020learning." fig-alt="Sim-to-Real Robotic Transfer Setup with Digital Twin Simulation. Authentic experimental apparatus for vision-based dexterous in-hand manipulation from OpenAI's Dactyl project [@andrychowicz2020learning]. (Left) The physical experimental cage housing a 24-DoF anthropomorphic Shadow Dexterous Hand, surrounded by 16 PhaseSpace infrared motion-tracking cameras and 3 Basler RGB cameras for ground-truth state validation and multi-view vision. (Right) The high-throughput MuJoCo simulated digital twin environment used to train reinforcement learning policies across billions of synthetic transitions. Robust sim-to-real transfer is achieved by applying extensive domain randomization over surface friction, joint damping, actuator force gains, link and object masses, object dimensions, visual lighting, and camera parameters, together with modeled motor backlash and action delay, forcing the neural policy to treat unmodeled physical variations as noise while operating within the supported deployment envelope. Attribution: @andrychowicz2020learning."}
![](images/jpg/fig06_real_sim2real_dactyl.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

::: {#ws-training-dactyl-tendon-snap .callout-war-story title="Sim-to-real hardware breakage (2018)"}
**Context**: OpenAI trained a reinforcement learning policy entirely in a randomized MuJoCo simulation to reorient a block in a 24-DoF Shadow Dexterous Hand, whose joints are driven through tendons by motors in its base [@andrychowicz2020learning].

**Mechanism**: The simulated hand applied torque directly at its joints, while the physical hand is tendon-actuated and has substantial backlash. The authors smoothed every action with an exponential moving average, in simulation and on the robot, to avoid abrupt changes in the action signal that could harm the physical hand.

**Impact**: The authors report robot breakages during the physical experiments, most often at the wrist's vertical joint, probably because it carries the largest load. Each repair took time and often changed aspects of the system, so the physical results were collected at different times, and the authors count hardware breakage among the key challenges of the work.

**Response**: The team also trained a second policy with the wrist pitch joint locked, and it transferred better to the physical hand.

**Systems lesson**: A simulator that neither wears nor breaks cannot price hardware exposure into the reward. The limits that protected the hand, an action filter and a locked joint, were imposed outside the learned policy, and every repair changed the plant on which the policy was being evaluated.
:::

::: {#fig-06-simulation-scaling fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Selected simulation throughput examples**: Illustrative steps-per-second values for different simulators, tasks, hardware, and execution settings. The points show why parallel accelerator designs can support large rollout budgets; they are not a controlled longitudinal benchmark or a universal scaling law." fig-alt="Log-scale scatter plot of eight selected simulation throughput examples from 2012 to 2024. Points span single-core CPU, multicore CPU, GPU, and TPU configurations with different workloads; unconnected markers avoid implying directly comparable year-to-year improvements."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mlsysim import viz

data = pd.read_csv("vol4/06_training/data/simulation_throughput_scaling.csv")

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(9, 5.5))
ax.scatter(data['year'], data['sps'], s=90, color=COLORS["primary"])

# Custom offsets: (dx, dy, ha, va)
offsets = [
    (-10, 18, 'right', 'bottom'),  # 2012 MuJoCo
    (15, 18, 'left', 'bottom'),  # 2013 Bullet
    (-15, 15, 'right', 'bottom'),  # 2017 MuJoCo Ray
    (-15, 15, 'right', 'bottom'),  # 2019 Isaac Gym
    (-15, 15, 'right', 'bottom'),  # 2021 Brax
    (15, -22, 'left', 'top'),  # 2022 Isaac Gym Preview 4
    (-15, 15, 'right', 'bottom'),  # 2023 MuJoCo MJX
    (0, -18, 'center', 'top'),  # 2024 Isaac Lab
]

for i in range(len(data)):
    dx, dy, ha, va = offsets[i]
    plt.annotate(
        f"{data['simulator'].iloc[i]}\n({data['hardware'].iloc[i]})",
        (data['year'].iloc[i], data['sps'].iloc[i]),
        textcoords="offset points",
        xytext=(dx, dy),
        ha=ha,
        va=va,
        fontsize=9,
        color=COLORS["primary"],
        arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='-', color=COLORS["grid"], lw=0.8, alpha=0.7) if abs(dx) > 10 or abs(dy) > 15 else None,
    )

plt.yscale('log')
plt.xlabel('Year of Introduction', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Simulation Throughput (Steps per Second)', fontsize=12)
```
