: **Multidimensional sim-to-real reality gap taxonomy**: Decomposition of the dynamics, sensing, and timing channels of the reality gap, with dynamics split into actuator and contact rows; appearance is sized in the prose and in panel (d) of @fig-06-sim2real-gap. Columns specify the unmodeled physical phenomenon, representative quantitative discrepancy, the latent control shortcut exploited by the optimizer, illustrative paired-trace acceptance criteria, and candidate mitigations. The listed values are scenario assumptions, not measured latch discrepancies or universally qualified thresholds. {#tbl-06-reality-gap tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

For the latch, repeated training against one plate stiffness can teach a response that depends on that exact value. Domain randomization varies modeled quantities during training so the policy encounters a range of plausible responses. The parameter distribution states which variations receive training weight; it does not certify every member of that range. This can be interpreted as **Bayesian regularization over physical dynamics distributions**.[^fn-math-domain-randomization] In nominal reinforcement learning, a policy optimizes expected return over a single simulation model parameterized by vector $\boldsymbol{\xi}_0$:
$$J(\boldsymbol{\theta}; \boldsymbol{\xi}_0) = \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\tau \mid \boldsymbol{\xi}_0)} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^T \gamma^t r(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t) \right].$$
In Domain Randomization, the physical environment is instead framed as a prior distribution over plausible Markov Decision Processes parameterized by physical variables $\boldsymbol{\xi} \sim p(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ spanning link masses, centers of mass, friction coefficients, joint damping, actuator latency, and sensor noise variances. The DR objective optimizes expected return marginalized over this physical parameter prior:
$$J_{\text{DR}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \mathbb{E}_{\boldsymbol{\xi} \sim p(\boldsymbol{\xi})} \left[ J(\boldsymbol{\theta}; \boldsymbol{\xi}) \right] = \int_{\Xi} \left( \mathbb{E}_{\tau \sim p_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\tau \mid \boldsymbol{\xi})} \left[ \sum_{t=0}^T \gamma^t r(\mathbf{s}_t, \mathbf{a}_t) \right] \right) p(\boldsymbol{\xi})\,d\boldsymbol{\xi}.$$
Marginalizing over $p(\boldsymbol{\xi})$ rewards performance across sampled parameter settings rather than only at the nominal model. A high average return can still conceal poor behavior in a low-probability part of that distribution. Expected-return optimization therefore establishes no stability guarantee across its entire support. A different objective optimizes the least favorable modeled parameter setting through minimax control:
$$\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \min_{\boldsymbol{\xi} \in \Xi} J(\boldsymbol{\theta}; \boldsymbol{\xi}),$$
The inner minimum selects the lowest modeled return within the uncertainty set $\Xi$, while the outer maximum seeks a policy that improves that result. Even this objective is a statement about return under the specified model and reward, not a physical stability proof. The engineering choice is which variations to model and weight, followed by closed-loop tests of the resulting behavior. Neither averaging nor worst-case optimization supplies evidence for an omitted mechanism.

Two limits guide that choice. A plant outside the sampled support ($\boldsymbol{\xi}_{\text{real}} \notin \text{supp}(p(\boldsymbol{\xi}))$) has not been represented by the training distribution. An omitted mechanism, such as backlash or scheduling jitter, remains absent even if the modeled masses and friction coefficients vary widely. Broader parameter ranges can also force a policy that cannot identify the active dynamics to compromise between incompatible responses. That compromise can cost precision or throughput without resolving the omitted mechanism.

[^fn-math-domain-randomization]: **Bounded support of domain randomization**\index{Domain randomization!support boundary}: Domain randomization optimizes expected return over parameter variations $\xi \sim \mathcal{P}(\Xi)$. Any generalization claim extends only over the support of $\mathcal{P}(\Xi)$ and says nothing about dynamics omitted from the simulator's equations of motion. On a mechanism with unmodeled transmission compliance or bus jitter, the policy treats those dynamics as unexplained noise and can fall into a high-frequency limit cycle.

Within the mechanisms the simulator does model, randomization has a useful width, a **domain randomization corridor**\index{Domain randomization!corridor}. Too narrow a distribution leaves the policy brittle against the variation the plant actually shows, which risks mechanical shock or a thermal trip, and too wide a distribution drives it toward conservative, low-gain control that gives up throughput. Keeping randomization inside that corridor rather than tuning it by trial takes a fixed order of work. System identification on the physical bench measures the nominal masses, torque constants, delays, and friction first. The randomization bounds are then grounded in the mechanisms that move those parameters, such as winding temperature for the torque constant and surface condition for friction, rather than in heuristic intervals. Training begins in a narrow band around the nominal values and widens it only as the policy meets its declared success threshold, the schedule known as adaptive domain randomization. Finally, paired traces audit every channel against its tolerance, and a discrepancy past budget sends the simulator back for revision before any policy trained on it is deployed.

What randomization cannot reach, the permission path must bound. Every proposal passes the permission path (@sec-boundary-machine-model) before it reaches an actuator, and there force-rate clamps, torque slew limits, and velocity governors hold it to what its validated sensing and stopping assumptions cover.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The sub-millisecond Control Barrier Function filters bounding unverified policy proposals are formulated in @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention.
:::

Decomposing the gap into its constitutive physical channels yields two concrete engineering artifacts, namely a supported region and an explicit residual mismatch list. The supported region is the set of conditions within which physical hardware matches simulation within validated tolerances. The residual mismatch list itemizes every unclosed difference that remains outside the training distribution. For the latch simulator, paired probes have not yet closed the strike-plate contact stiffness, which its penalty spring sets far softer than the plate, or the actuator transport lag, so both head its residual list, and the supported region excludes the contact states those two departures govern. Each entry on the residual list defines an explicit requirement for runtime monitors and safety filters, which must detect when physical execution drifts past the boundary where the simulated policy remains valid. Both artifacts pass into the policy manifest of @sec-training-policy-manifest: the residual list enters its omission log, and every state outside the supported region is entered there as an exclusion.

### Teacher-student privileged state distillation and asymmetric actor-critic {#sec-training-privileged-distillation}

Simulation exposes quantities a deployed policy may never observe directly, such as the true friction at a contact. Training can use that extra information, but the deployed proposer must act from the sensors installed on the machine. In actor-critic learning, the actor proposes actions and the critic estimates their future reward to guide training. An asymmetric design gives the critic more information than the actor; a teacher-student design instead trains an informed teacher and then teaches a sensor-limited student to imitate it. Both require checking that the student's available observations support the behavior being learned.

The difficulty is **partial observability** (POMDP). Identical measured joint angles and velocities can precede different returns when a footpad is slipping on oil or braced against dry concrete. A critic $V_{\boldsymbol{\phi}}(\mathbf{o}_t)$ that sees only the instantaneous observation cannot distinguish these conditions. Simulation can expose the hidden contact wrenches $\mathbf{w}_c$, friction $\mu$, terrain, and payload inertia to the training algorithm, improving the information available for value estimation without requiring those inputs in the deployed actor.

Asymmetric actor-critic and teacher-student distillation use that extra training information differently [@lee2020learning; @kumar2021rma]. In the asymmetric design, the actor receives only the sensor history it will have at deployment, while a privileged critic supplies training feedback. The critic is discarded at deployment. In the two-phase arrangement of @fig-06-privileged-distillation, a teacher first learns with privileged inputs; the student then learns to reproduce its actions from runtime observations. The second design adds a transfer problem because some distinctions available to the teacher may be unavailable to the student. Privileged information can improve training feedback, but it does not eliminate value-estimation error or make hidden state observable on the machine.

For the latch, the student can compare commanded effort with the resulting motion over recent observations. A different response can reveal a changed contact or load. Yet the same response can have multiple causes, and an unobserved strike-plate offset cannot be inferred merely because a teacher knew it. A temporal encoder supplies a learned estimate whose accuracy must be checked against physical measurements. An auxiliary training loss can ask it to predict simulator parameters, but that objective creates no information absent from the sensor history.

::: {#fig-06-privileged-distillation fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Teacher-student privileged state distillation**: A schematic two-phase transfer pipeline. The teacher uses simulator state during training, and the student learns from onboard observations and their history. The training advantage does not establish that every privileged quantity is identifiable from those observations. The deployed student still requires physical validation, and its output remains a proposal to the independent permission path, omitted from this schematic." fig-alt="Two-panel systems diagram. Left panel shows Phase 1 with a physics simulator providing privileged state s_priv (friction, contact forces, elevation, mass) to an RL teacher policy. Right panel shows Phase 2 with real onboard sensors passing proprioception and vision to a sliding temporal history buffer, which feeds a student policy running on edge silicon, with an arrow indicating supervised distillation from teacher to student."}
![](images/svg/fig06_privileged_distillation.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The history length must resolve the changes relevant to the task without obscuring their onset. A short window may not distinguish a changed load from noise; a long one increases storage and inference work and can leave an encoder dominated by observations preceding contact. This is an estimator-design trade-off, not a universal short- or long-window threshold. For the latch candidate, qualification must check contact-onset response under the chosen history length and measured sensing delays. Retaining a long history need not itself delay the newest observation, but the trained estimator must use that observation promptly.

Even under careful domain randomization, contact calibration, and privileged state distillation, residual discrepancies persist in high-precision, contact-rich regimes, and the latch simulator's residual list is not yet empty. Some local mismatches can be addressed by learning on the physical fixture. That choice spends wear and requires new evidence for the updated checkpoint.

## Real-Robot Fine-Tuning and Residual Control {#sec-training-real-machine-tuning}

The real cage door carries its strike plate at a small structural mounting offset from where the simulator placed it, a departure the simulator does not model. A local, measurable mismatch of this kind is what fine-tuning on physical hardware can absorb. Gradient updates computed from physical rollouts adapt the policy to the true compliance, contact dynamics, and bus delays of the machine, but they measure none of those mechanisms, so the simulator's other two departures, the soft contact spring and the missing transport lag, stay in the omission log until paired probes close them. The adaptation also has a physical price. In a simulator, sampling states near the boundary of stability costs only compute cycles, while on hardware every sample expends component life and risks driving the machine into an unrecoverable contact state.

The cost of updating policy parameters on physical hardware\index{Fine-tuning!on physical hardware} compounds, because the gradient steps that solve localized contact errors also consume finite mechanical fatigue life, heat the motor windings, and risk catastrophic forgetting of pre-verified nominal transit stability.

```{python}
#| label: calc-training-latch-residual-exposure
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LATCH RESIDUAL FINE-TUNING EXPOSURE
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: The real-machine fine-tuning example that follows (latch-res-03).
# │ Goal: Convert an on-robot interaction budget into contact time and threshold samples.
# │ Show: setpoint period and rate, active contact time, above-threshold sample count.
# │ How: RM.chunk_step (machine setpoint period); AISLE.f_latch_tripwire;
# │      step count and exceedance fraction are scenario assumptions.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class LatchResidualExposure:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────
    t_step = RM.chunk_step  # category: chosen (setpoint period of the chunk policy)
    f_trip = AISLE.f_latch_tripwire  # category: illustrative (contact tripwire on the latch)
    plate_offset = 1.5 * millimeter  # category: illustrative (real plate position vs. simulated placement)
    n_steps = 20_000  # category: illustrative (interaction steps collected)
    frac_exceed = 0.015  # category: illustrative (exploratory steps past the tripwire)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────
    f_step = (1 / t_step).to(hertz)
    t_active = (n_steps * t_step).to(second)
    n_exceed_samples = round(n_steps * frac_exceed)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────
    check(abs(t_step.to(millisecond).magnitude - 25.0) < 1e-9, f"setpoint period {t_step}")  # M5 (was 20 ms)
    check(abs(f_step.to(hertz).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"setpoint rate {f_step}")
    check(abs(t_active.to(second).magnitude - 500.0) < 1e-6, f"active time {t_active}")
    check(n_exceed_samples == 300, f"above-threshold samples {n_exceed_samples}")
    check(abs(f_trip.to(newton).magnitude - 15.0) < 1e-9, f"tripwire {f_trip}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ───────────────────
    t_step_str = fmt_latency(t_step, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_step_str = fmt_frequency(f_step, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    n_steps_str = fmt_int(n_steps)
    t_active_str = fmt_latency(t_active, unit=second, precision=0)
    frac_exceed_pct_str = fmt_percent(frac_exceed, precision=1, style="prose")
    n_exceed_samples_str = fmt_int(n_exceed_samples)
    f_trip_str = fmt_force(f_trip, precision=0)
    plate_offset_str = fmt_length(plate_offset, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

Consider adapting `latch-sim-02` into `latch-res-03`, a residual candidate that adds a gated learned correction to the frozen `latch-sim-02` output, because the real plate sits `{python} LatchResidualExposure.plate_offset_str` from where the simulator placed it. The mechanism guides the spring-loaded latch past its strike plate, where non-smooth Coulomb friction, cam surface geometry, and spring preload produce sharp stick-slip transitions. The policy's setpoints arrive every `{python} LatchResidualExposure.t_step_str` (`{python} LatchResidualExposure.f_step_str`). To adapt its parameters to the contact dynamics of the strike plate, an on-robot fine-tuning routine collects an illustrative `{python} LatchResidualExposure.n_steps_str` interaction steps, representing `{python} LatchResidualExposure.t_active_str` of active contact and near-contact operation. Stochastic exploration can generate force transients within the response delay of the low-level controller. If `{python} LatchResidualExposure.frac_exceed_pct_str` of sampled steps exceed the `{python} LatchResidualExposure.f_trip_str` contact tripwire, the run contains `{python} LatchResidualExposure.n_exceed_samples_str` above-threshold samples. Consecutive samples can belong to one sustained contact; they do not establish that many distinct impacts. Event segmentation and force-time traces are needed to count shocks and assess their severity.

Any resulting impacts load the drivetrain, and assigning that exposure a fraction of service life requires a drive-specific load-spectrum and life model (@sec-body-actuator-limits)\index{Cycloidal drive!fatigue life}. Heat is the second constraint. Exploration dither raises the root-mean-square current through the motor coils, and that Joule heating\index{Joule heating!actuator thermal limits} can bring the winding to its derating threshold (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles) within minutes unless the training schedule budgets cooling intervals.

An improvement on the contact fixture does not establish an improvement over the whole task. A parameter update $\Delta\boldsymbol{\theta}$ produces a new checkpoint, while prior trial results remain observations of the earlier policy $\theta_0$\index{Statistical verification!collapse under fine-tuning}. Those results are not erased, but extending their claim to the new policy requires evidence. Updates that reduce local contact error can change free-space behavior or stopping proposals in regions absent from the adaptation data\index{Catastrophic forgetting!in physical fine-tuning}. Because physical trials consume time and wear, requalification must target both the intended improvement and the behaviors the update could disturb.

The updated checkpoint therefore needs its own configuration record and regression evidence. During adaptation, the permission path must also cover the intermediate policies produced by the optimizer. Localizing the learned correction reduces the scope of behavior that those updates can directly change.

### Residual policy architectures and bounded authority {#sec-training-residual-architectures}

A residual policy can localize adaptation without changing the frozen base policy weights. The proposed control input is
$$\mathbf{u}_{\text{prop}}(\mathbf{s}) = \pi_{\text{base}}(\mathbf{s}) + g(\mathbf{s})\,\Delta\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{s}),$$
where $\pi_{\text{base}}$ is the frozen base controller, $\Delta\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}$ is a learned contact correction, and an independently checked gate $g(\mathbf{s})\in\{0,1\}$ is one only inside the validated contact region. Qualification of the base and the combined controller is still required. In particular, the unqualified `latch-sim-02` does not become a qualified base merely by freezing its weights. The gate sets the residual *exactly* to zero in free space and outside that region; an absent reward gradient would not do so. The permission path checks the measured state and proposed combined input before actuation.

A training penalty such as $\|\Delta\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{s})\|^2$ merely encourages small corrections; the independent gate removes them where they are unauthorized. Even then, gate transitions, state estimation, timing, and shared actuator limits still belong in the combined controller's validation.

A magnitude limit $\|g(\mathbf{s})\Delta\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{s})\|\le\Delta_{\max}$ bounds one aspect of authority. The same path must enforce correction rate and state limits, actuator feasibility, and a fallback when sensing or the proposal expires. The allowed residual set must fit a validated robustness margin for the *combined* controller across the claimed operating region; comparing an arbitrary torque magnitude against a nominal stability margin is insufficient. For the latch fixture, we would admit correction only during the measured contact phase, with a zero-output free-space gate and a bounded torque slew. After each weight update, contact and free-space regression tests must recheck tracking, stopping, thermal load, and shock exposure before the new checkpoint receives authority. A clipped residual can still excite an oscillation or saturate a drive if these conditions fail.

Bounded residual authority limits a proposed correction but cannot by itself prevent hardware damage or eliminate latent failure modes from earlier training choices. Every stage of policy synthesis, from demonstration ingestion through the simulation contact solver to residual updates, leaves its own failure signature in the controller's closed-loop behavior, and each signature can be traced back to the training assumption that produced it.

## Policy Optimization Pathology and Training Failure Modes {#sec-training-failure-modes}

A physical failure in a learned policy is rarely arbitrary. The command that drives an end-effector into a strike plate was produced by optimization over a specific dataset, loss, and simulator, and the assumptions of that optimization leave a structural footprint that can be traced before the machine runs. The **policy vulnerability inference chain**\index{Policy vulnerability inference chain}\index{Vulnerability analysis!training regimes} makes the trace explicit in five links ($\text{Exposure} \to \text{Dependency} \to \text{Violated Assumption} \to \text{Observable Signature} \to \text{Permission-Path Interceptor}$). The training exposure establishes a learned dependency, a deployment condition violates it, the violation produces a signature in the commands or the plant, and the signature names the interceptor the permission path requires. Each of the three latch checkpoints runs the chain once.

For `latch-bc-01`, the teleoperated openings of @sec-data support the nominal plate at the guarded approach; the campaign never demonstrated a displaced plate. A sagged door violates that dependency. The signature is compounding covariate shift\index{Covariate shift!in behavioral cloning}, although individual proposals can remain physically plausible until the gripper binds. A support monitor must compare the measured condition against the supported cells and refuse policy authority outside them. The predeployment test follows from the known absence in the occupancy join (@sec-data-policy-coverage): displaced-plate bench trials must establish whether the monitor trips before binding.

For `latch-sim-02`, simulated door openings teach dependence on soft contact and absent command lag. The real plate violates those assumptions, producing the overforce transient quantified in @sec-training-simulator-component. Paired contact probes expose the mismatch before deployment. When the contact deadline leaves insufficient time to stop, the interceptor must act before contact. The stopping envelope ($v_{\text{safe}}(z) \le \sqrt{2 a_{\text{brake}} z}$) preserves a stop before the plate; guarded contact needs the separate qualification described in @sec-training-contact-exploit. A force tripwire remains useful, but detecting a force excursion does not establish that the actuator can arrest it.

For `latch-res-03`, adaptation concentrates experience on one rig's contact states. Improvement there leaves behavior elsewhere untested, with regression\index{Catastrophic forgetting!fine-tuning regression} a possible signature. The frozen contact and free-space suite must pass before the new weights receive authority, and the residual gate holds the correction at zero outside the measured contact phase. The shock and winding heat incurred during exploration (@sec-training-real-machine-tuning) also require monitoring, even when the task reward improves.

The simulation and residual lineage leaves unresolved dependencies until evidence closes them; a later training stage does not automatically repair an earlier one. The recovery-imitation branch takes a different route. `latch-bc-recovery-02` adds attributable corrections for a named displaced-plate condition without depending on the unqualified simulator. Its remaining uncertainty concerns the resulting closed-loop behavior and nominal regression, which the qualification request makes explicit.

Each chain connects a training assumption to a targeted test and an execution limit. The policy manifest preserves those connections with the checkpoint's source data, simulator, objective, and modifications, so evaluation can test the candidate's specific dependencies.

## The Policy Manifest {#sec-training-policy-manifest}

The candidate selection must distinguish nominal behavior supported by demonstrations, newly taught recovery, and contact behavior that still depends on unverified simulation. The failure chains make that distinction concrete for each checkpoint. The record accompanying the candidate into evaluation preserves the reasoning, including the assumptions that remain open.

The **policy manifest**\index{Policy manifest!definition} records how a checkpoint was produced: its training stages, the data support it inherits from the provenance records, its simulator versions and the **omission log**\index{Policy manifest!omission log} of mechanisms they leave out and mismatches paired probes have not closed, the wear incurred during adaptation, and the operating domain it declares (@tbl-06-training-schema). These fields state what evaluation must test and what runtime enforcement must accommodate. The runtime safety supervisor (@sec-enforcement) can check the manifest against its validated configuration before enabling a checkpoint. A declared boundary does not automatically generate a reliable detector or a safe clamp; those mechanisms require their own engineering and evidence.

The manifest separates optimization results from the conditions the policy may be asked to operate in\index{Operational design domain!training boundaries}. The **declared ODD** is the part of the ODD from @sec-data-policy-coverage that the policy manifest claims: the supported cells of the data join, minus every state the omission log excludes. High training reward or low offline loss does not show that the policy is safe outside it, so the declared ODD is computed from the join and the log, never from the training curve, and a convergent metric cannot stand in for clearance over regimes nobody characterized.

The separate `latch-bc-recovery-02` manifest consumes the original provenance and the stipulated `latch-recovery-02` archive. It adds the positively displaced-plate cell at the guarded approach to the candidate domain, with the expert recovery labels and held-out sessions identified by digest. Its qualification request asks whether the updated policy completes that recovery and preserves nominal service under the same physical limits. The original archive remains unchanged. Negative displacement and the fast approach remain excluded. Current provenance bounds the evidence already available; collecting and qualifying new experience can expand the machine's useful competence.

| Record Schema Field             | Physical / Computational Data Modality                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Provenance & Immutability Guarantee                                                      | Downstream Verifier & Usage                                                                                                       |
|:--------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **`regime_sequence`**           | Array of optimization stages ($\text{BC} \to \text{SimRL} \to \text{Distill} \to \text{Residual}$), loss formulas, teacher privileged state dimensions ($\mathbf{w}_c, \boldsymbol{\xi}$), student observation history horizon $H$, reward weights, and stopping criteria hashes | Git commit SHA, PyTorch/JAX checkpoint UUIDs, parameter hash $H(\theta_k)$               | Tracing which regime introduced latent failure modes or high-gain chatter                                                         |
| **`policy_inference_contract`** | Model architecture class, parameter count, checkpoint weights hash $\text{hash}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, chunk prediction horizon $H_p$, execution horizon $H_a$, denoising/ODE steps $K$, inference deadline $t_{\text{chunk}}$, and chunk lease $T_{\text{lease}}$               | Cryptographic checkpoint hash $\text{hash}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, compiled engine digest | Parameterizes the runtime proposal buffer (@sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline) and real-time lease monitor (@sec-nervous-lease-sizing) |
| **`data_support_ledger`**       | Digests of the consumed provenance records and of the scenario ledger they were measured against; the `supported_cells` and `known_absences` of their occupancy join                                                                                                             | Cites each provenance record by digest; no dataset field is copied                       | Upper bound on the declared ODD; parameterizes out-of-distribution support monitors                                               |
| **`negative_event_registry`**   | Authority-record entries (@sec-data-intervention-recovery) from training and adaptation rollouts                                                                                                                                                                                 | Cites each authority-record entry by digest; its pre-trigger trace is not copied         | Isolating physical failure boundaries and preventing corrupted drift rollouts from training                                       |
| **`simulation_provenance`**     | Physics engine build, integrator method, timestep $\Delta t$, contact solver penalty parameters, and domain randomization ranges $\mathcal{P}(\Xi)$                                                                                                                              | Physics engine binary hash, URDF/MJCF asset tree hash                                    | Reproducing the training physics and auditing paired-trace budgets                                                                |
| **`omission_log`**              | Mechanisms each simulator leaves out (backlash, compliance, transport lag) and the residual mismatches paired probes did not close, with the states each one affects                                                                                                             | Bound to the simulator build it describes; an entry closes only on paired-trace evidence | Removes the states it affects from the declared ODD; carried into evaluation's coverage gaps and the fault list                   |
| **`adaptation_wear_ledger`**    | Serialized hardware IDs, contact shock counts, motor current RMS thermal logs, modified layer indices, and regression suite hash                                                                                                                                                 | Calibration certificate hashes, hardware lifetime fatigue logs                           | Re-opening formal qualification cases and preventing silent regression of nominal capabilities                                    |
| **`declared_odd_boundary`**     | Declared ODD: the supported cells minus the states the omission log excludes (for the latch policy, the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach speed)                                                                                                                      | Never exceeds the supported cells of `data_support_ledger`                               | Bounds the target ODD that evaluation may sample and the region in which the permission path admits policy proposals              |

: **Policy manifest schema**: Fields the policy manifest adds to the provenance records it consumes, recording policy synthesis stages, inference execution parameters, data support by digest, physics engine specifications and their omission log, hardware fine-tuning wear, and the declared ODD. {#tbl-06-training-schema tbl-colwidths="[20,18,22,40]"}

For the original latch campaign and its simulation-residual lineage, a compact manifest links the fields into one decision:

- `regime_sequence`: demonstration checkpoint `latch-bc-01` → `latch-sim-02`, a student initialized from `latch-bc-01` and distilled from a simulator teacher trained by reinforcement learning on privileged state (privileged contact wrenches $\mathbf{w}_c$ distilled into an 8-step observation-history buffer) → gated residual candidate `latch-res-03`; retain each checkpoint hash, loss or reward specification, and stop rule.
- `policy_inference_contract`: specify checkpoint weights hash $\text{hash}(\boldsymbol{\theta})$, the machine's `{python} DecoderBudget.act_params_str`-parameter ACT architecture with one decoder pass per chunk, chunk prediction horizon $H_p =$ `{python} DecoderBudget.horizon_str` setpoints at `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_step_str`, and the `{python} DecoderBudget.t_act_str` P99 inference target; record the selected execution prefix separately from the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.t_chunk_str` proposal-renewal deadline and the lease selected in @sec-nervous-lease-sizing. Each renewed prefix requires valid evidence and a feasible continuation or fallback; the prediction horizon is not the active lease.
- `data_support_ledger`: cite the latch campaign's provenance records and its scenario ledger by digest; their join supports the nominal strike plate at the guarded approach, and lists the displaced plate and the faster approach, whose cells hold no demonstrations, as known absences with no recovery label.
- `simulation_provenance`: record the actual solver build and contact parameters.
- `omission_log`: the example simulator models strike-plate contact with a penalty spring far softer than the plate and omits actuator transport lag, so the contact states those two departures govern are unverified for the checkpoints trained in simulation.
- `negative_event_registry`:\index{Negative event registry}\index{Pre-trigger ring buffer} cite by digest the authority-record entry, with its pre-trigger ring-buffer trace, for every fixture-shoulder strike, operator veto, or permission-path clamp with its event classification, without treating rejected learner commands as expert targets, and mark episodes an operator truncated so that an update does not score an aborted command as a success.
- `adaptation_wear_ledger`:\index{Adaptation wear ledger} associate `latch-res-03` with the specific rig, above-threshold samples and separately identified contact events, motor-current history, modified residual weights, and free-space regression result.
- `declared_odd_boundary`: the supported cells minus the states the omission log excludes, here the nominal plate at the guarded approach of `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_guarded_str`. The contact states governed by the two omissions stay outside the declared ODD for every simulation-refined checkpoint, `latch-sim-02` and `latch-res-03` alike, until paired probes close them. The displaced plate and the `{python} LatchContactDeadline.v_fast_str` approach lie outside it, and the fast approach would stay outside even with demonstrations, because its contact deadline (@sec-training-simulator-component) leaves almost nothing beyond the contact-loop response; there the permission path must impose the guarded approach or refuse policy authority.

A qualification review would withhold operational authority from `latch-res-03` until paired contact probes quantify the contact-stiffness error and the omitted lag, and the combined controller passes contact, free-space, stopping, and wear-budget tests. With only the original campaign, the same rule leaves `latch-bc-01` as the checkpoint evaluation may sample, provided the support monitor of its chain refuses policy authority off the nominal plate (@sec-training-failure-modes). Trained without a simulator, it carries no omission-log exclusions, so its declared ODD keeps the door's contact states at the nominal plate and the guarded approach. The manifest records that decision and its evidence rather than converting a training score into permission.

The manifest references the collector, plant, calibration, and action taps through the provenance record of @sec-data-schema. The cited digests preserve which data and coverage ledger produced the checkpoint; later changes require a new record rather than silently updating its lineage. Simulator provenance similarly fixes the solver and timestep[^fn-rule-sim-timestep] used during optimization. Its separate omission log carries unresolved discrepancies from @sec-training-sim-to-real-gap into evaluation's coverage gaps and fault-injection tests.

[^fn-rule-sim-timestep]: **Choosing a penalty-contact timestep**\index{Simulation!timestep bounds}: The needed step size depends on effective contact mass, penalty stiffness and damping, the integrator, and solver tolerances. The characteristic contact timescale changes with roughly $\sqrt{m_{\text{eff}}/k_{\text{eff}}}$; refine the timestep until contact onset, peak force, and impulse converge to the accuracy the task requires.

Downstream engineering teams consume the manifest throughout the design, evaluation, and release lifecycle. The evaluation record of @sec-evaluation-logs consumes it directly. Its target ODD is sampled from inside the declared ODD, and its catalog of coverage gaps inherits the known absences and the omission log, so evaluation suites probe the specific failure modes each training regime predicts. Targeted exploratory tests outside the candidate domain can also identify gaps, but they do not establish an operational claim there without new support and qualification. The permission path of @sec-enforcement takes the declared ODD as the outer limit of the region in which it admits policy proposals, and uses the recorded support to parameterize out-of-distribution detectors. Verification in @sec-verification and the safety case in @sec-release draw on the manifest to establish the provenance of every parameter update and to confirm that each omission is bounded by an independent physical interlock.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The policy manifest's omission log parameterizes adversarial fault-injection benches in @sec-verification-deriving-fault-list.
:::

::: {#chk-training-provenance-record .callout-checkpoint title="Policy manifests and declared ODDs"}

Before releasing a trained policy checkpoint to physical verification, verify your understanding of the policy manifest, its omission log, and the declared ODD:

- [ ] **Complete the latch record**: A fixture-shoulder strike appears after `latch-res-03` was trained with a soft penalty contact and no actuator lag. Which omitted mechanism belongs in `omission_log`, and which paired probe and admission decision must the manifest record?
- [ ] **Confining the declared ODD**: Suppose demonstrations were collected at the fast approach and every omission-log entry were closed by paired probes. Why would the latch policy's declared ODD still exclude the fast approach, which timing comparison decides it, and what must the permission path impose on a proposal that arrives at that speed?
- [ ] **Negative event logging**: Why does the manifest keep the pre-trigger trace of an operator veto or fixture strike as labeled failure evidence rather than as an imitation target?
- [ ] **Declared operational boundaries**: `latch-bc-01` proposes to open the door while the strike plate sits displaced from its nominal mount. How does the permission path use the data support ledger to classify that state as ungrounded extrapolation rather than demonstrated competence, and why does a confident policy output not change the classification?
:::

The manifest turns a training history into a claim with stated limits. The original record sends `latch-bc-01` to evaluation and keeps `latch-res-03` out of service until paired probes and regression tests close its gaps. The stipulated recovery record sends `latch-bc-recovery-02` with a wider, explicitly testable candidate claim. The common ways that decision goes wrong all let a training score stand in for that evidence.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-training-fallacies-pitfalls}

Minimizing loss on an offline demonstration split, or maximizing simulated return, measures compliance with the training environment rather than competence on the machine. When the objective rewards behavior that exploits data curation or simulator approximations, the ranking of candidate policies established in training inverts on deployment\index{Deployment!policy ranking inversion} (@fig-06-policy-ranking-inversion), because the virtual environment forgives maneuvers that real hardware does not. Before a trained policy receives actuator authority, the causal assumptions linking its training metrics to physical outcomes must be stress-tested.

::: {#fig-06-policy-ranking-inversion fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative policy ranking inversion**: (a) A constructed slope graph shows how a candidate favored by a simulated score can lose its advantage under physical evaluation. (b) Possible causes include unsupported recovery states, contact mismatch, and actuator chatter. The rankings are a teaching example, not measured results for the latch checkpoints." fig-alt="A schematic slope graph shows candidate rankings changing between simulation score and hardware yield, beside diagrams of state drift, contact force, and actuator chatter."}
![](images/svg/fig06_policy_ranking_inversion.svg){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Sanitizing recovery episodes to achieve lower offline validation loss.*\index{Validation!data sanitization}

Suppose the latch archive also held recovery runs, and two cage-door latch policies train on different versions of it. One retains the recovery runs, in which the operator backed the gripper off and re-seated it after the latch cam caught on the strike plate; the other removes them and achieves a lower loss on its own held-out split. When the cam catches on the machine, the first policy backs off and re-seats, while the second keeps pushing along the demonstrated path until the permission path's contact tripwire halts the mechanism. Because the sanitized dataset lacks examples of correcting from errors, the lower loss merely reflects an artificially simplified test set, not better physical disturbance handling\index{Disturbance rejection!recovery data}. Scrubbing the recovery data has made the mathematical prediction task easier at the direct expense of removing the corrective behavior the deployed controller physically needs. **Removing recovery trajectories to optimize offline prediction loss strips the policy of the only data demonstrating how to escape compounding error.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Retain authority-record entries and curate attributable expert recovery trajectories as training targets. Never filter demonstration datasets solely to minimize validation MSE, and mandate closed-loop perturbation benchmarks to evaluate recovery capability before releasing checkpoints.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Transitioning from human demonstrations to simulation reinforcement learning removes the failures training left in the policy.*\index{Reinforcement learning!regime transition failures}

An assembly team replaces behavioral cloning with simulation reinforcement learning to correct lateral drift during gasket seating. The new policy eliminates the drift but seats the mechanism with $65\text{ Hz}$ torque chatter, which the simulator's massless-rotor assumption permits because it ignores the inertia the motor must reverse. On the physical machine the chatter excites drivetrain resonance\index{Actuation!mechanical resonance} and heats the stator windings to their derating threshold through $I^2R$ losses\index{Thermal management!Joule heating} (@sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles), so the drives derate and most seatings fail to complete. The training change addressed one failure mechanism and exposed another, so evaluation must follow the complete task through contact and repeated operation and check the assumptions the new regime introduced as carefully as the data limitations it replaced. **Simulation does not erase inductive vulnerabilities; it trades human data limitations for numerical solver shortcuts and contact relaxations.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Require paired-trace validation across all four reality gap channels before deploying sim-trained policies, and enforce hardware rate-limiters and low-pass action filters ($f_{\text{cutoff}} \le 20\,\text{Hz}$) to prevent high-frequency chatter from unmodeled rotor inertia.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Treating behavioral cloning as standard offline supervised learning.*\index{Behavioral cloning!I.I.D. regression fallacy}

An engineer trains a behavioral cloning policy on 500 expert demonstrations, achieves an impressive $0.005$ validation loss on held-out demonstration splits, and declares the controller production-ready. On hardware deployment, the robot drifts off course within three seconds and collides with a fixture. The engineer diagnoses a capacity bottleneck and adds transformer layers. In physical feedback systems, the independent and identically distributed ($i.i.d.$) assumption of supervised learning fails because the robot's action $\mathbf{a}_t$ directly determines its next observation $\mathbf{o}_{t+1}$. A microscopic tracking error $\epsilon$ shifts the robot into an observation state slightly outside the demonstration support; with no training signal on how to return, later actions can increase the deviation. Under the imitation-learning bound's assumptions, worst-case accumulated task cost can grow as $\mathcal{O}(T^2 \epsilon)$; this does not specify the growth of physical displacement or collision probability. Furthermore, when human demonstrations exhibit multimodal strategies—such as evading an obstacle by steering left or right—fitting a unimodal regression head with mean squared error forces the policy to output the conditional expectation $\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{a}\mid\mathbf{o}]$, commanding a fatal straight-line trajectory directly into the obstacle. Offline validation loss evaluates accuracy exclusively along human-visited trajectories where squared errors to opposing modes balance out; it does not by itself establish closed-loop stability or obstacle clearance after displacement. **Validation loss measures accuracy only along human-visited trajectories, providing zero mathematical guarantee of closed-loop stability or multimodal obstacle avoidance.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Deploy runtime state-support monitors (such as Mahalanobis distance in latent space or kernel density estimators) on the permission path to intercept ungrounded extrapolation before compounding drift induces collisions, and mandate expressive multimodal action decoders (diffusion, flow matching, or GMMs) whenever demonstration datasets contain topological path bifurcations.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming online gradient updates preserve predeployment safety envelopes.*\index{Statistical verification!collapse under fine-tuning}

When a sim-to-real transferred policy exhibits a steady-state positioning error on a physical assembly jig, an engineer enables online fine-tuning on the robot. After 5,000 steps, the local contact error is eliminated. The team assumes the policy is strictly superior. However, modifying weights $\Delta\theta$ creates a new checkpoint; the earlier simulation trials remain evidence for their original configuration. While local contact accuracy improved, the gradient steps can induce catastrophic forgetting in unvisited regions, degrading high-speed free-space transit stability or corrupting emergency braking profiles. Physical time and wear constrain the regression campaign, so its scope must follow the behaviors the update could affect. **Evidence for earlier weights does not automatically establish the updated checkpoint's behavior; qualification must cover the change and its possible regressions.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Restrict real-world adaptation strictly to gated residual policy architectures ($u = \pi_{\text{base}} + g(s)\Delta\pi$) with an externally enforced binary gate ($g(s) \equiv 0$ in free space), and mandate frozen non-regression suites that verify tracking and stopping profiles before granting authority.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Believing that widening parameter distributions can substitute for missing physical mechanisms.*\index{Domain randomization!panacea fallacy}

To overcome sim-to-real transfer failures, an engineering team widens domain randomization bounds to extreme intervals—randomizing link masses by $\pm 50$ percent and friction coefficients across $[0.05, 1.5]$. The resulting policy fails to complete precision assembly tasks on real hardware, moving sluggishly and hesitating at contact. Parameter randomization operates strictly within the differential equations the simulator already models. It cannot synthesize an omitted physical dynamic, such as transmission backlash, Stribeck friction, or transport jitter. Forcing a policy to remain optimal across unphysical parameter spreads merely dilutes network capacity, driving it toward overly conservative, low-gain control that sacrifices operational throughput without resolving the missing causal mechanisms. **Wider parameter ranges do not add an omitted mechanism; they change the distribution over mechanisms the simulator already represents.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Ground domain randomization bounds in physical bench measurements (adaptive domain randomization corridors) and explicitly log omitted mechanisms in the policy manifest's omission log, retaining only operating conditions that independent limits can cover under validated physical assumptions.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming multi-step generative decoders can execute synchronously within inner actuator control loops.*\index{Diffusion policy!inference latency wall}

An ML engineer replaces a unimodal regression head with a 16-step diffusion policy, observing superior multimodal trajectory modeling in offline simulation benchmarks. When deployed to a $50\,\text{Hz}$ ($20\,\text{ms}$) hardware control loop, the robot exhibits catastrophic motion jitter and runaway stall trips. Under the illustrative assumption that the weights do not remain in cache at batch size $B=1$, each sequential denoising step ($K=16$) streams the parameter footprint ($M$ bytes) across the memory bus, bounding inference throughput by the memory wall ($t_{\text{compute}} \ge K \cdot M / b_{\text{mem}}$). For a $100\,\text{MB}$ diffusion head running on a $68\,\text{GB/s}$ memory bus, 16 steps consume $23.5\,\text{ms}$ in raw DRAM weight streaming alone—exceeding the $20\,\text{ms}$ actuator cycle even if arithmetic overlaps weight transfers. The bandwidth lower bound alone is enough to reject this synchronous schedule; it is not a claim that memory transfer and arithmetic occur in separate phases. Attempting synchronous per-step denoising blows past real-time deadlines, dropping motor setpoints and triggering hardware watchdog halts. **A decoder that overruns its deadline needs fewer evaluations, a different implementation, or asynchronous execution under an independently validated lease.**

**Architect's countermeasure**: Decouple iterative inference from inner actuator execution when the measured decoder latency requires it. Record the prediction horizon, executed prefix, proposal-renewal deadline, and active lease separately under the qualified contract of @sec-nervous-lease-sizing. Buffering does not extend permission: the execution path checks current evidence and state and invokes its qualified fallback on expiry.

:::

## Summary {#sec-training-summary}

Every training regime buys a capability and leaves a dependency in the weights. Behavioral cloning depends on the states its demonstrators visited and can average incompatible action choices; simulation depends on its contact model, timing, and omitted mechanisms; fine-tuning depends on recent experience and requires evidence for the updated checkpoint. A training score alone does not expose those dependencies. Tracing each one to a possible failure identifies what evaluation must test and what independent execution limits must cover. The policy manifest records that reasoning and confines the declared operating domain accordingly. Principle \ref{pri-vol4-endogenous-drift} requires attention to the states a policy's own corrections reach, while simulation adds a second kind of absence: mechanisms its solver never represented.

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Policy synthesis and sim-to-real transfer"}
* **Every regime leaves a dependency no training score shows:** Offline loss and simulated return reward compliance with the data and the solver. Candidate rankings can therefore invert on hardware, and a deployment condition that violates a dependency produces a predictable failure signature that names the detector the permission path needs.
* **Mode choice and recovery are separate problems:** Regression can average valid alternatives into an invalid action, while successive errors can reach states the demonstrations omit. A multimodal decoder addresses the first problem; recovery experience and closed-loop evidence address the second. Independent runtime limits remain necessary for both.
* **Decoder latency must fit the proposal contract:** Repeated model evaluations increase latency and memory traffic. When a decoder cannot meet the synchronous deadline, asynchronous chunk playback needs a validated lease and fallback. A more expressive action distribution does not earn extra time at the actuator.
* **Training information must survive the sensor boundary:** Privileged simulation state can guide learning, but the deployed student sees only its runtime inputs. Observation history helps only where different physical conditions leave distinguishable traces; distillation does not remove the need for calibration and transfer testing.
* **Randomization covers parameters, not missing mechanisms:** Domain randomization broadens training over dynamics the simulator already models, and paired probes size the remaining gap channel by channel. An omitted backlash, compliance, or transport delay stays omitted and enters the omission log.
* **Fine-tuning spends wear and reopens qualification:** Physical rollouts consume component life, and evidence collected for earlier weights does not automatically apply to the updated checkpoint. A gated residual limits where adaptation acts, but the combined controller still requires regression tests and independent execution limits.
* **A wider declared ODD needs new support:** The policy manifest cites the current data by digest and excludes conditions affected by unresolved omissions. New attributable recovery experience can support a broader candidate domain; closed-loop qualification must establish the behavior claimed there.
:::

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From policy manifests to evidence"}
How much can a finite run of clean trials establish about a checkpoint whose manifest already limits where it may be trusted? @Sec-evaluation takes the policy manifest as its input. Its illustrative campaign begins with twenty nominal door runs of `latch-bc-01` and asks what that finite sample establishes. A separate stipulated branch takes `latch-bc-recovery-02` through nominal regression and displaced-plate qualification, showing what additional evidence would support useful recovery under the guarded approach.
:::
